source: Lessons 1 to 20: first written from the school Science curriculum journey 2026-27 and Pearson Edexcel GCSE schemes, re-mapped to 4BI1 Biology 2, 4CH1 Chemistry 1 and 4PH1 Physics 1 (microscopy lesson 3 retired as not on the International GCSE); demonstrations replace hands-on practicals for online delivery; INSET lesson standard | Edexcel IGCSE 4BI1/4CH1 specification summary (content/syllabus/ks4/gcse-science.json), Y10 units Biology 1, Biology 2, Chemistry 1, Chemistry 2. Drive material not used. Not re-taught because covered by the lessons 1 to 20 in content/lessons/gcse-science/y10.json: animal, plant and bacterial cell structure and levels of organisation, specialised cells, differentiation and stem cells, enzymes with temperature and pH and the active site, food tests, diffusion, osmosis and active transport (Biology 2 points 1-3 mostly); states of matter and changes of state, purity and melting points, mixtures and separation, chromatography and Rf, atomic structure and isotopes, relative atomic mass, Periodic Table groups, periods and electronic configurations (Chemistry 1 points 1-4 mostly). Gaps remain in solubility curves and gas diffusion, which are taught here. | Edexcel IGCSE Physics 4PH1 specification (units Physics 1-4, Y10). Existing UK-GCSE lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y10.json already cover Physics 1 points on distance-time and velocity-time graphs, average speed, acceleration and v² = u² + 2as, resultant force, F = ma and W = mg, stopping distance and Hooke's law, so those points are not re-taught here; this file adds vectors/scalars, terminal velocity, momentum and moments. | Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology 4BI1 / Double Award 4SD0 specification | Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1 (and Science Double Award 4SD0) specification | Spring 1 2027 (bridge weeks 11 and 18 Jan: lessons 1, 4, 12, 15, 16, 6, 74, 39, 17, 18 upgraded; Spring 1 weeks 1 to 3: 75, 26, 60, 96, 27, 36, 28, 37, 58, 98 upgraded and 105 to 109 new): Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Science (Double Award) 4SD0 and the school's Pearson GCSE five-year schemes (only 4SD0 content); home practicals with written guides | Spring 2 2027 (lessons 76, 25, 43, 62, 110, 31, 29, 44, 64, 32, 45, 65, 84, 46, 66, 63, 33, 34, 111, 48, 102, 112, 92, 113, 114, 115; weeks of 15 Mar to 19 Apr, 5, 4, 3, 4, 5, 5 lessons): 4SD0 Biology 2, Chemistry 2 and Physics 3 (Double Award points only; kidney, transpiration, titration and lead(II) sulfate are not taught), with exam-style questions written for these lessons; teacher demonstrations on camera for laboratory reagents; home practicals with household items and written safety guides

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Animal, plant and bacterial cells
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a plant cell need a cell wall but an animal cell does not?
objectives: To understand how the structures in animal, plant and bacterial cells relate to their functions
successCriteria: All: label the structures of an animal and a plant cell
Most: state the function of each structure
Some: compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells using correct exam terms
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: chloroplasts and the energy changes of photosynthesis
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order inside every cell as a sign of the Creator

keywords.def: contains genetic material that controls the cell
site of aerobic respiration
site of photosynthesis
cellulose layer that supports a plant cell
small ring of DNA in bacteria

hook.text: A single bacterium has no nucleus, yet it can copy itself every 20 minutes. How can it manage without one?
hook.a: Its DNA is free in the cytoplasm as a loop, with extra plasmids; it still has ribosomes to make proteins.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We have certainly created the human being in the best of forms' (at-Tin 95:4). Studying how cells and organs work is a way of recognising that design.

starter.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
Name the levels of organisation from smallest.
starter.a: Organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system

starter.q: Which structures are found only in plant cells?
starter.a: Cell wall, chloroplasts, large permanent vacuole

teach.heading: Levels of organisation
bullets: Organelles → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems
teach.note: Edexcel International GCSE Biology (4BI1 2.1) requires this sequence.

teach.heading: Cell structures
bullets: Know each structure and its job
teach.note: Answer the big question: both have nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes because all cells need control, exchange, reactions and energy.

head: Structure
Function
Plant
Animal
rows: contains genetic material; controls the cell

teach.heading: Bacterial cells (prokaryotic)
bullets: No nucleus: chromosomal DNA free in the cytoplasm
Cell wall, membrane, ribosomes; some have a flagellum
teach.note: 4BI1 1.3 lists the features of bacterial cells. Bacteria are much smaller (about 1 to 5 µm) than animal cells (about 10 to 30 µm).

teach.heading: Exam wording
teach.note: Mark schemes reject 'make energy'.

misconception.wrong: Mitochondria produce energy
misconception.right: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy

teach.heading: Check: structure
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which structure is found in both plant and animal cells?
check.why: Ribosomes make proteins in all cells. The others are plant-only.

practice.q: Give two differences between a plant cell and an animal cell. [2 marks]
practice.a: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall (1); chloroplasts (1) (or a large permanent vacuole).
practice.model:
Name a structure and say which cell has it.
Point 1: plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells do not.
Point 2: plant cells have chloroplasts for photosynthesis; animal cells do not.

practice.q: State the function of the cell membrane. [1 mark]
practice.a: Controls what enters and leaves the cell.

practice.q: Where is the DNA in a bacterial cell?
practice.a: Free in the cytoplasm (a loop) and in plasmids.

independent.q: Core: Draw and label a palisade (plant) cell and a cheek (animal) cell with seven structures and one function each.
independent.a: Nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes in both; cell wall, chloroplasts, vacuole in the plant cell.
independent.model: Teacher labels the nucleus first: 'Nucleus: contains genetic material (DNA) that controls the cell's activities.'

independent.q: Extend: Compare a bacterial cell with a plant cell. [4 marks] Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Both have a cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes (1); bacteria have no nucleus, DNA is a loop (1); bacteria have plasmids (1); bacteria have no chloroplasts or mitochondria (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why a root hair cell has no chloroplasts. [2 marks]
independent.a: It is underground with no light (1), so it cannot photosynthesise; chloroplasts would be no use (1).

exit.q: Which structure is NOT found in an animal cell?
Big question: why does a plant cell need a cell wall but an animal cell does not?
exit.a: The cellulose wall supports the plant cell and keeps it firm; animals are supported by skeletons instead.

lessons.homework: Make a revision card comparing animal, plant and bacterial cells (portal flashcards).
lessons.send: SEND: labelled diagram with a word bank. EAL: organelle names with function sentences. Stretch: explain why red blood cells have no nucleus.

the tip of a sperm cell containing enzymes to digest the egg's outer layer

starter: Bismillah. Name the site of aerobic respiration.
What does the nucleus contain?

teach.heading: Three specialised cells (4BI1 2.5B)
bullets: Learn the cell, its job and its adaptations

head: Cell
Function
Adaptations
rows: haploid nucleus; acrosome with enzymes; many mitochondria; tail
haploid nucleus; nutrients in cytoplasm; membrane changes after fertilisation

teach.heading: Explaining an adaptation
bullets: Structure → what it does → how it helps the function
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Explain how a sperm cell is adapted to reach and fertilise an egg (4 marks)
steps: Many mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration
This powers the tail to swim towards the egg
The acrosome contains enzymes to digest the egg's outer layer
The haploid nucleus combines with the egg's nucleus to restore the full number of chromosomes
model.answer: Two adaptations, each linked to the function

misconception.right: Many mitochondria release energy through aerobic respiration for swimming

teach.heading: Check: adaptation
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: What is the function of the acrosome?

lessons.title: Enzymes: temperature and pH
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a high fever become dangerous?
objectives: To understand how temperature and pH affect the activity of enzymes
successCriteria: All: describe enzymes as biological catalysts with an active site
Most: explain the effect of temperature using collisions and denaturing
Some: analyse enzyme rate data and plan the amylase practical
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: catalysts and rates of reaction
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the precise conditions in the body that keep enzymes working

keywords.def: a biological catalyst made of protein
the part of the enzyme the substrate fits into
the molecule an enzyme acts on
active site changed shape so the enzyme no longer works
the condition at which the enzyme works fastest

hook.text: Your body temperature stays close to 37 °C. What might happen to your enzymes at 42 °C?
hook.a: Enzymes start to denature: active sites change shape, so vital reactions slow down.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, all things We created with precise measure' (al-Qamar 54:49). Chemistry's calculations rest on the fact that substances always react in fixed, measurable proportions.

starter.a: Speeds up a reaction without being used up.

starter.q: Name the iodine test result for starch.

teach.heading: Lock and key
teach.note: Animation of specificity.

teach.heading: Temperature
teach.note: Answer the big question: above about 40 °C, body enzymes begin to denature.

model.problem: Explain the shape of an enzyme activity, temperature graph (4 marks)
steps: As temperature rises, molecules have more kinetic energy
More successful collisions between enzyme and substrate
Peak at the optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes)
Above it, bonds in the enzyme break, active site changes shape: denatured

teach.heading: pH
bullets: Each enzyme has an optimum pH
teach.note: Extremes of pH denature enzymes too.

teach.heading: Practical: amylase and temperature
bullets: Dependent: time for starch to disappear (iodine test)
teach.note: Show the demo video with a spotting tile.

misconception.wrong: Enzymes are killed at high temperatures
misconception.right: Enzymes are proteins, not alive; they are denatured

teach.heading: Check: denature
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Why does activity fall above the optimum temperature?
options: The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
check.why: Heat breaks bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer matches the substrate.

practice.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme reaction falls above its optimum temperature. [3 marks]
practice.a: The active site changes shape (1); the enzyme is denatured (1); the substrate no longer fits, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).
practice.model:
Point 1: high temperature breaks bonds holding the enzyme's shape.
Point 2: the active site changes shape: denatured.
Point 3: the substrate no longer fits, so the rate falls.

practice.q: Pepsin works best at about pH 2. Where in the body is it found?
In the amylase practical, what is the dependent variable?
practice.a: Time for starch to disappear (iodine stays orange-brown).

independent.q: Core: Amylase data: 20 °C: 300 s; 30 °C: 150 s; 40 °C: 90 s; 50 °C: 200 s; 60 °C: no reaction. Calculate rate (1000 ÷ time) and describe the pattern.
independent.a: Rates: 3.3, 6.7, 11.1, 5.0, 0; rises to an optimum near 40 °C then falls; enzyme denatured at 60 °C.
independent.model:
Teacher works the first: 1000 ÷ 300 = 3.3 s⁻¹.
Then reads the trend: rate increases up to 40 °C.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why the rate increases from 20 to 40 °C. [2 marks]
independent.a: More kinetic energy (1), so more frequent successful collisions between enzyme and substrate (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Plan how to find the optimum pH of amylase. [4 marks] Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Buffers at several pH values (1); same temperature in a water bath, same volumes (1); test drops with iodine every 10 s until no blue-black (1); compare times, repeat (1).

exit.q: An enzyme that has changed shape and no longer works is...
Big question: why does a high fever become dangerous?
exit.a: Enzymes begin to denature, so the reactions that keep cells alive slow down.

lessons.homework: Complete the enzyme graph question on the portal (plot rate against temperature).
lessons.send: SEND: lock-and-key cut-out model. EAL: active site, substrate, denature. Stretch: explain enzyme action using collision theory.

lessons.title: Diffusion, osmosis and active transport
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do chips go floppy in salty water?
objectives: To understand how substances move into and out of cells by diffusion, osmosis and active transport
successCriteria: All: define diffusion, osmosis and active transport
Most: explain the potato osmosis results
Some: calculate percentage change in mass and find the concentration of no net movement
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: concentration and particle movement
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the balance of water in living things

keywords.def: net movement of particles from high to low concentration
net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane
movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
lets some molecules through but not others
difference in concentration between two areas

hook.text: Root hair cells take in mineral ions even when there are more ions inside the cell than in the soil. How?
hook.a: Active transport, using energy from respiration.

starter.q: Which process needs energy from respiration?
Name the structure that controls what enters a cell.

teach.heading: Three processes
teach.note: Display and refer to throughout.

teach.heading: The potato osmosis practical
bullets: Equal potato cylinders in sucrose solutions
teach.note: Show the demonstration video.

model.problem: A cylinder goes from 2.50 g to 2.20 g in 0.6 mol/dm³ sucrose. Find the % change and explain.
steps: The solution was more concentrated than the cell contents
Water left the cells by osmosis

teach.heading: Finding the cell concentration
bullets: Where the line crosses 0%, no net osmosis
teach.note: That concentration equals the concentration inside the potato cells.

teach.heading: Water moves, not sugar
bullets: In osmosis only water crosses the membrane
teach.note: Common error.

misconception.wrong: Sugar moves into the potato, so it gains mass
misconception.right: Water moves in or out by osmosis; the solute stays outside

teach.heading: Check: osmosis
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A potato cylinder gains mass in pure water. Why?
check.why: Pure water is more dilute than the cell contents, so water enters by osmosis.

practice.q: A potato cylinder goes from 2.50 g to 2.80 g. Percentage change? [2 marks]
practice.model:
Change = final - initial = 2.80 - 2.50 = 0.30 g.
Divide by the start mass: 0.30 ÷ 2.50 = 0.12.
Multiply by 100: +12%.

practice.q: Explain why the cylinder gained mass. [2 marks]
practice.a: The solution was more dilute than the cell contents (1), so water moved in by osmosis (1).

practice.q: Give one difference between diffusion and active transport.
practice.a: Active transport needs energy (and goes against the gradient); diffusion does not.

independent.q: Core: Data: 0.0 M: +15%; 0.2 M: +6%; 0.4 M: -3%; 0.6 M: -11%; 0.8 M: -18%. Plot % change against concentration and find where the line crosses 0%.
independent.a: Line crosses 0% at about 0.33 M: the potato cell concentration.
independent.model: Teacher plots the first two points and explains: positive means water entered by osmosis.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why chips go floppy in salty water. [3 marks]
independent.a: Salt solution is more concentrated than the cell contents (1); water leaves cells by osmosis (1); cells lose turgor and become flaccid (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Suggest why we calculate percentage change rather than change in mass.
independent.a: Cylinders start at different masses; percentage change allows fair comparison.

exit.q: Osmosis is the movement of...
Big question: why do chips go floppy in salty water?
exit.a: Water leaves the potato cells by osmosis into the more concentrated salt solution.

lessons.homework: Do the potato and salt water test at home with an adult (two potato chips, one in plain water, one in salty water, 30 minutes). Compare their firmness.
lessons.send: SEND: comparison table of the three processes. EAL: gradient, membrane, permeable. Stretch: explain osmosis in terms of water potential.

check.why: F = 5 × 4 = 20 N. A and D divide; B adds.

practice.q: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 3 m/s². Resultant force? [2 marks]
practice.model:
Formula: F = m × a.
Substitute: 1200 × 3.
Calculate: 3600.
Unit: N.

practice.q: Weight of a 60 kg pupil on Earth?
A 2000 N force acts on a 500 kg boat. Acceleration?

independent.q: Core: Six F = ma and W = mg questions (portal worksheet), including one on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg).
independent.a: Answers in worksheet key, e.g. 70 kg on the Moon: 112 N.
independent.model: Teacher does question 1: a 0.5 kg ball, a = 20 m/s²: F = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N.

independent.q: Extend: A 900 kg car has a driving force of 2500 N and drag of 700 N. Find its acceleration. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain the difference between mass and weight. [2 marks]
independent.a: Mass is the amount of matter in kg and does not change (1); weight is the gravitational force in N and depends on g (1).

exit.q: Weight is measured in...
Big question: why is it harder to push a full trolley?
exit.a: Greater mass needs a greater force for the same acceleration (F = ma).

lessons.homework: Complete the F = ma and weight question set on the portal.

Explain why braking distance increases more than speed

keywords.def: distance travelled during the driver's reaction time
distance travelled once the brakes are applied
thinking distance + braking distance
time taken to respond to a hazard

starter: F = ma: 1000 kg, 3 m/s²
Distance at 20 m/s for 0.7 s
Name something that slows reactions
What is friction?

teach.heading: Two parts
teach.note: Highway Code data at 30 mph: thinking 9 m + braking 14 m = 23 m.

teach.heading: Factors
bullets: Thinking: tiredness, phone use, alcohol, drugs
Braking: wet or icy roads, worn tyres or brakes, heavy load
teach.note: Answer the big question: thinking distance doubles with speed; braking distance roughly quadruples.

teach.heading: Calculating thinking distance
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A driver at 15 m/s has a reaction time of 0.6 s; braking distance is 18 m. Find the stopping distance.

teach.heading: Phones affect thinking, not braking
bullets: Wet roads affect braking, not thinking
teach.note: Classic exam distinction.

misconception.wrong: Wet roads increase thinking distance
misconception.right: Wet roads increase braking distance; distractions increase thinking distance

teach.heading: Check: factor
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which increases braking distance but not thinking distance?
check.why: Ice reduces friction between tyres and road. The others slow the driver's reactions.

practice: Define stopping distance
Two factors affecting thinking distance
Thinking distance at 20 m/s, reaction 0.5 s

Factor that increases thinking distance?
Why are lower limits used near schools?

Describe the practical to investigate extension of a spring
Identify the limit of proportionality

Plot and interpret force–extension graphs
Distinguish elastic and plastic deformation and explain the limit of proportionality

keywords.def: increase in length from the original length
extension is directly proportional to force, up to a limit
point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to force
returns to original shape when the force is removed

starter: Weight of 0.5 kg mass?
What does 'directly proportional' mean?
Stopping distance = ?
Gradient of a straight line through the origin

teach.heading: The practical
bullets: Add 1 N weights one at a time
teach.note: 4PH1 practical (1.22): show the demo video. Read the ruler at eye level.

model.problem: A spring is 5.0 cm long. With 3 N added it is 8.6 cm. Find the extension.

teach.heading: Force–extension graph
bullets: Straight line through the origin: Hooke's law
Curves after the limit of proportionality
teach.note: Answer the big question: equal force steps give equal extensions, so the scale on a newtonmeter is even.

teach.heading: Elastic vs plastic
teach.note: Compare a spring and plasticine.

teach.heading: Length vs extension
teach.note: Common data error.

misconception.wrong: Plot total length against force
misconception.right: Plot extension (length − original length) against force

teach.heading: Check: Hooke
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A spring extends 2 cm for 4 N. Below its limit, what is the extension for 10 N?
check.why: 0.5 cm per N, so 10 N gives 5 cm. Extension is proportional to force.

practice: Extension: original 12 cm, new 15.5 cm
Sketch a force–extension graph with a limit
Define elastic deformation
independent: Core: Calculate extensions from a results table and plot the graph
Extend: Identify the limit of proportionality from data and explain your choice
Stretch: Evaluate the practical: sources of error and how to reduce them.

Extension: 20 cm → 23 cm?
What happens beyond the limit of proportionality?

lessons.unit: Biology 1: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Characteristics of living organisms and the eukaryote groups
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes something alive, and how do biologists sort the living world?
objectives: State the eight characteristics of living organisms
Describe the features of plants, animals, fungi and protoctists
Classify an organism from a description of its cells and nutrition
successCriteria: All: name the characteristics and the four eukaryote groups
Most: describe the key features of each group with an example
Some: classify an unfamiliar organism and justify using evidence
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: biodiversity across habitats
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the variety of life; stewardship (khilafah) means caring for what we classify

keywords.def: organism whose cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
mostly single-celled eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus, e.g. Amoeba
removal of toxic waste and substances in excess of requirements
taking in materials for energy, growth and development

starter: Bismillah. Name two structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.
What is the function of the nucleus?
In which organelle does aerobic respiration take place?

teach.heading: Eight characteristics of life
bullets: Every living thing shows all eight, at some point
Use them as a checklist for 'alive or not?'
teach.note: Ask pupils to shout out a verb for each: move, respire, sense, control, grow, reproduce, excrete, feed. Stress that excretion is not the same as egestion (removing undigested food). Check against the specification wording for the eighth characteristic (control of internal conditions) before printing.

head: Characteristic
Meaning
Example
rows: action causing a change of position or place
a plant leaf turning to the light
chemical reactions in cells releasing energy from nutrients
keeping conditions in the body steady
permanent increase in size and dry mass
making more of the same kind
removing toxic waste or excess substances
taking in materials for energy and growth

teach.heading: The four eukaryote groups
bullets: All eukaryote cells have a nucleus
Groups differ in cell walls, chloroplasts and feeding
teach.note: Walk across the table row by row. Ask: which feature separates fungi from plants? (chitin walls, no chloroplasts, absorb food). Point out that protoctists are a mixed group and that Chlorella has chloroplasts but is not a plant because it is single-celled.

head: Group
Cell wall
Chloroplasts
Nutrition
Examples
rows: feed on other organisms; store glycogen
absorb nutrients from dead or living matter

teach.heading: Model: classify the organism
bullets: Look for cell wall material first
Then chloroplasts, then how it feeds
teach.note: Think aloud: match each clue to the table. Ask pupils which single clue would be enough to rule out 'plant' (no chloroplasts).

model.problem: Organism X is multicellular. Its cells have nuclei and cell walls made of chitin, no chloroplasts. It grows as thread-like hyphae through stale bread and absorbs nutrients. Which group is it?
steps: Nuclei, so it is a eukaryote
Chitin wall and no chloroplasts rules out plants
Hyphae and absorbing nutrients is typical of fungi
Mucor is a fungus that grows on bread

teach.heading: Common error: fungi are plants
bullets: Fungi were once grouped with plants
teach.note: Ask where a mushroom gets its energy. Many pupils think fungi 'grow in soil like plants'.

misconception.wrong: A mushroom is a plant because it grows from the ground.
misconception.right: Fungi have chitin cell walls and no chloroplasts, and absorb nutrients from dead matter, so they are not plants.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils see 'chloroplasts' and say plant. Chlorella is single-celled and classified as a protoctist.

check.q: Chlorella is a single-celled organism with a nucleus and chloroplasts. It is best classified as:
check.why: It has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote; being single-celled with chloroplasts places it with the protoctists. Plants are multicellular and prokaryotes have no nucleus.

practice: A mushroom grows on a log, takes in nutrients, releases spores and grows larger over a week. Which characteristics of life does it show?
Mucor has hyphae and no chloroplasts. Amoeba is single-celled and moves by pseudopodia. State one feature that is the same and one that is different.
Explain why a flame is not classed as living even though it grows and uses oxygen. [3 marks]
independent: Core: Copy and complete a table giving cell wall, chloroplast and nutrition for plants, animals, fungi and protoctists.
Extend: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. Explain why it is not a protoctist. [3 marks]
Stretch: A student says a crystal growing in a saturated solution is alive because it grows. Evaluate this using all eight characteristics.
exit: Name the four groups of eukaryotes. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: give two characteristics a car engine shows and two that it does not.
lessons.homework: Revise the table of eukaryote groups; make 8 flashcards for the characteristics.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded characteristic cards with picture prompts. Stretch: ask why viruses are debated as living.

lessons.unit: Biology 1: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Prokaryotes, pathogens and viruses
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a medicine kill bacteria but not a virus?
objectives: Describe the features of bacteria as prokaryotes
Name the four types of pathogen with an example disease each
Describe viruses as non-living particles
successCriteria: All: name pathogen types and a disease each
Most: describe bacterial and viral structure
Some: compare sizes and explain why antibiotics fail against viruses
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: hygiene and preventing infection
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: tahara (cleanliness) as protection of health; gratitude for the body's defences

keywords.def: single-celled organism with no nucleus; DNA free in the cytoplasm
organism that causes disease
small circle of DNA found in bacteria
non-living particle with genetic material in a protein coat; reproduces only inside host cells

starter: Bismillah. List the four eukaryote groups.
State two features of a eukaryotic cell.
Convert 3 mm to micrometres.

teach.heading: Bacteria: prokaryotes
teach.note: Show a labelled bacterium. Ask what is missing compared with an animal cell (nucleus, mitochondria). Mention that some bacteria are useful (Lactobacillus makes yoghurt) and some harmful (Pneumococcus causes pneumonia).

left.title: Bacterium (e.g. Lactobacillus, rod-shaped)
points: No nucleus; DNA loose in cytoplasm

teach.heading: Four types of pathogen
bullets: A pathogen is anything that causes disease
teach.note: Ask pupils to guess how each spreads. Malaria: the pathogen Plasmodium is carried by Anopheles mosquitoes (the vector).

teach.heading: Viruses are not cells
bullets: Genetic material inside a protein coat
No cytoplasm, no nucleus, no respiration
Only reproduce inside a host cell
teach.note: A virus shows reproduction only when inside a host, so it is described as non-living. Examples: tobacco mosaic virus (plants), influenza, HIV.

model.problem: A bacterium is 2 µm long. An influenza virus is 100 nm across. How many times longer is the bacterium?
steps: Convert to the same unit: 2 µm = 2000 nm

teach.heading: Why antibiotics do not work on viruses
bullets: Viruses live inside our own cells and have none
teach.note: Link forward to the antibiotic resistance lesson in Year 11. Pupils often say antibiotics 'fight infections'; be precise.

misconception.wrong: Antibiotics cure all infections, including colds and flu.
misconception.right: Antibiotics kill bacteria only. Colds and flu are caused by viruses, which have no bacterial structures to target.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: 'reproduces on its own' sounds alive; insist that a virus has no cell and replicates only in a host.

check.q: Which statement about viruses is correct?
options: They reproduce on their own in water
They have a cell wall and cytoplasm
They reproduce only inside host cells
check.why: Viruses have no cellular structure and replicate only in a host cell, so they are described as non-living particles.

practice: Name the pathogen type for malaria and for athlete's foot.
Draw and label a bacterium with four parts.
A bacterium is 3 µm long and a virus is 60 nm. How many times longer is the bacterium?
independent: Core: Make a table of the four pathogen types with an example and disease.
Extend: Compare a bacterial cell and a virus in four points. [4 marks]
Stretch: Explain why an antibiotic given for a viral infection would be harmful as well as useless.
exit: Why are viruses not classed as living organisms? [2 marks]
Return to the big question in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word explanation for a younger pupil of why viruses are not living cells.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled diagram bank. Stretch: research how TMV was discovered.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Photosynthesis and limiting factors
lessons.bigQuestion: What stops a plant from photosynthesising faster?
objectives: Write word and balanced equations for photosynthesis
Describe how light, CO₂ and temperature limit the rate
Describe an investigation using pondweed
successCriteria: All: write the word equation
Most: balanced equation and explain limiting factors
Some: design and evaluate the pondweed investigation and read graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: balancing equations; Geography: food security
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on how plants turn sunlight into food for all life; stewardship of crops

keywords.def: process in which plants use light energy to make glucose from CO₂ and water
green pigment that absorbs light energy
the factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate of a process
how quickly something happens, e.g. bubbles per minute

starter: Bismillah. Name the green pigment in chloroplasts.
What is the formula for carbon dioxide?
What is an enzyme?

teach.heading: The equations
teach.note: Say that light energy is not a reactant but it is written over the arrow. Check balancing: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O on each side. Ask what happens to the glucose: respiration, starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, lipids in seeds, amino acids with nitrate.
cycle: Water arrives from roots via xylem
Oxygen leaves; glucose is used or stored

teach.heading: Limiting factors
bullets: The factor in shortest supply sets the rate
teach.note: Use the 'queue at the till' analogy: more tills do not help if you are waiting on a stock-check. Temperature beyond about 45 degrees Celsius denatures the enzymes of photosynthesis, so the rate falls.

teach.heading: Model: pondweed data
bullets: Count bubbles per minute at set distances
Control temperature with a water-bath screen
teach.note: Method: pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, lamp at measured distance, wait 2 minutes, count bubbles for 1 minute, repeat three times and average. Variables: independent is distance; dependent is bubbles per minute; control CO₂, temperature, same piece of weed. Safety: keep the lamp and mains away from water.

model.problem: Mean bubbles per minute at lamp distances: 10 cm: 48, 20 cm: 30, 30 cm: 18, 40 cm: 10. Describe the trend and give a reason.
steps: Read the values as the lamp moves away
Rate falls from 48 to 10 as distance increases
Greater distance means lower light intensity
Light is the limiting factor, so photosynthesis slows
model.answer: As the lamp moves further away, light intensity falls and the rate of photosynthesis decreases.

teach.heading: Reading limiting-factor graphs
bullets: Rising section: the plotted factor is limiting
Flat section: another factor is limiting
teach.note: Ask: at the plateau, what could you change to raise the rate? Pupils must name a different factor from the one on the x-axis.

misconception.wrong: At the flat part of the graph, adding more of the plotted factor will keep raising the rate.
misconception.right: At the plateau another factor is limiting, so only changing that factor will raise the rate.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. At the plateau in bright light, light is not limiting and CO₂ has stopped limiting; at 10 °C enzymes are slow, so temperature is. Pupils who pick light have misread 'bright'.

check.q: A plant in bright light at 10 °C has a photosynthesis rate that levels off as CO₂ concentration rises above 0.10%. What is probably limiting the rate now?
check.why: Light is already bright and CO₂ is no longer limiting at the plateau, so the low temperature (slow enzymes) is limiting.

practice: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis and count atoms on each side.
Why does the pondweed need sodium hydrogencarbonate in the water?
Name three control variables for the lamp-distance investigation.
independent: Core: Use the data to plot rate against distance and describe the pattern.
Extend: A grower raises CO₂ in a glasshouse but yield does not rise. Give two possible reasons. [2 marks]
Stretch: Design a plan to find out whether green light is used as well as red light. [4 marks]
exit: State the three limiting factors. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: how could a farmer decide which factor to raise?
lessons.homework: Learn the word and symbol equations; do 6 questions on limiting factor graphs.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: equation strips to sequence. Stretch: explain light intensity and distance using the inverse relationship.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Leaf structure, gas exchange in plants and mineral ions
lessons.bigQuestion: How is a leaf built like a tiny factory?
objectives: Describe the structure of a leaf and link it to function
Explain gas exchange in plants in light and dark
State the roles of nitrate and magnesium ions and the effects of deficiency
successCriteria: All: label a leaf section
Most: explain adaptations and net gas exchange
Some: interpret hydrogencarbonate indicator results and starch tests
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: pH indicators; Agriculture: fertilisers
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the quiet design of a leaf; moderation in fertiliser use as part of stewardship

keywords.def: pores in the leaf surface that let gases in and out
tightly packed cells at the top of a leaf with many chloroplasts
cell that opens and closes a stoma
needed to make chlorophyll

starter: Bismillah. Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
Name two limiting factors of photosynthesis.
What does a xylem vessel carry?

teach.heading: Inside a leaf
bullets: Palisade layer is near the light and full of chloroplasts
Spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas diffusion
teach.note: Draw on the board a cross-section top to bottom: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll with air spaces, lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells; xylem and phloem in the vein. Ask why most stomata are on the lower surface (cooler, less water loss).

head: Part
Adaptation
Function
rows: lets light reach the palisade layer
CO₂ in, O₂ and water vapour out

teach.heading: Gas exchange in light and dark
bullets: Day: photosynthesis is faster than respiration
Net result: CO₂ taken in, O₂ released
Night: only respiration, so O₂ in, CO₂ out
teach.note: Emphasise that plants respire all the time. Hydrogencarbonate indicator: red at normal CO₂, yellow if CO₂ rises, purple if CO₂ falls. Leaf in light turns purple; leaf in dark turns yellow; tube with no leaf stays red (control).

teach.heading: Model: explain an adaptation
teach.note: Model the three-part pattern: feature, effect, link. Pupils then reuse it in practice.

model.problem: Explain how the palisade layer is adapted for photosynthesis. [3 marks]
steps: Feature: cells are tightly packed at the top of the leaf
Effect: they absorb the most light as it enters
Feature: they contain many chloroplasts with chlorophyll
Link: so more light energy is absorbed for photosynthesis
model.answer: Packed near the surface with many chloroplasts, they absorb most light, so the rate of photosynthesis is high.

teach.heading: Mineral ions and the starch test
bullets: Nitrate makes amino acids and proteins
Deficiency: yellow leaves; nitrate also gives stunted growth
teach.note: Starch test: boil leaf 1 minute (stops reactions), hot ethanol in a water bath with no naked flame (removes chlorophyll), rinse in warm water, add iodine. Blue-black means starch. Variegated and foil-covered leaves show chlorophyll and light are needed.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils choose red ('no change') or purple ('it is a leaf'). In the dark there is only respiration, so CO₂ builds up and the indicator goes yellow.

check.q: A leaf in a tube with hydrogencarbonate indicator is wrapped in foil for 2 hours. The indicator is most likely to turn:
check.why: With no light there is no photosynthesis. Respiration releases CO₂, so the indicator turns yellow.

practice: Label the layers of a leaf from top to bottom.
Why does a leaf in the dark still use oxygen?
A farmer sees yellow leaves and stunted growth. Which ion might be short?
independent: Core: Explain how the leaf is adapted for gas exchange. [3 marks]
Extend: Explain why a variegated leaf with a white edge shows no starch there. [2 marks]
Stretch: A plant in a sealed bottle stays alive for months in light. Explain, using gas exchange. [4 marks]
exit: State the function of stomata and of guard cells. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: pick one part of the leaf factory and justify its design.
lessons.homework: Draw and annotate a leaf cross-section from memory.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: annotate a pre-drawn diagram. Stretch: how does a guard cell open the stoma?

lessons.title: The gut, peristalsis and absorption in the villus
lessons.bigQuestion: How does food get from your plate into your blood?
objectives: To understand how the alimentary canal moves food and how the small intestine is adapted for absorption
successCriteria: All: name the organs of the alimentary canal in order
Most: describe peristalsis and the role of each organ
Some: explain how the villus is adapted for absorption
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: surface area to volume ratio
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the Qur'an describes milk produced 'from between digested food and blood' (an-Nahl 16:66)

keywords.def: the tube from mouth to anus
waves of muscle contraction that push food along
finger-like projection of the small intestine wall
digested molecules passing into the blood
lymph vessel in a villus that absorbs fatty acids and glycerol

hook.text: Your small intestine is about 6 m long and folded inside you. Why might so much length be needed?
hook.a: More time and surface area to absorb digested food.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And indeed, in the grazing livestock is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between digested food and blood, pure milk' (an-Nahl 16:66). The gut and blood work together to turn food into what the body needs.

starter.q: Products of starch digestion by amylase?

starter.a: Net movement from high to low concentration.

teach.heading: A balanced diet
bullets: Vitamins and minerals for health; fibre; water
teach.note: Link to the Year 10 food tests lesson. Keep deficiencies concrete: vitamin C (scurvy), vitamin D with calcium (rickets, weak bones), iron (anaemia, low haemoglobin), fibre (prevents constipation). Energy needs vary with age, activity and pregnancy.

teach.heading: Enzymes of digestion
bullets: Amylase: starch → maltose, then maltase → glucose
teach.note: Amylase is made in the salivary glands and pancreas; protease (pepsin) works in the stomach at about pH 2; lipase and other enzymes work in the small intestine at about pH 8. Ask why the optimum pH differs.

teach.heading: Bile
bullets: Made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder
Emulsifies fat: more surface area for lipase
teach.note: Bile contains no enzymes. It does not digest fat chemically; it breaks it into droplets so lipase can work faster.

model.problem: Explain the role of bile in digestion. [3 marks]
steps: Bile is alkaline so it neutralises acid from the stomach
This gives the right pH for enzymes in the small intestine
It emulsifies fats into small droplets
So a larger surface area is available for lipase
model.answer: Neutralises acid and emulsifies fats, speeding up fat digestion.

teach.heading: The villus
bullets: Rich capillary network and a lacteal
Large surface area from villi and microvilli
teach.note: Link to diffusion and active transport: glucose and amino acids move into blood by diffusion and active transport; fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteal. A steep concentration gradient is kept by blood flow carrying nutrients away.

misconception.wrong: Nutrients are absorbed by diffusion only, so no energy is needed.
misconception.right: Glucose and amino acids also use active transport, which needs energy from respiration, especially when the gut concentration is lower than in the blood.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils pick the stomach because of acid. Bile is made in the liver and only stored in the gall bladder.

check.q: Where is bile made?
check.why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

practice.q: Put in order: stomach, oesophagus, small intestine, mouth, large intestine.
practice.a: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.
practice.model:
Start where food enters: mouth.
Swallowed down the oesophagus.
Mixed with acid in the stomach.
Digested and absorbed in the small intestine.
Water absorbed in the large intestine.

practice.q: What is peristalsis?
practice.a: Waves of muscle contraction that push food along the gut.

practice.q: Name the vessel in a villus that absorbs fatty acids.

independent.q: Core: Label a villus and write three adaptations with how each helps absorption.
independent.a: Thin wall one cell thick: short diffusion distance; rich capillary network: maintains the gradient; microvilli: large surface area; lacteal for lipids.
independent.model: Teacher labels the first: 'Wall one cell thick: short distance for digested molecules to diffuse into the blood.'

independent.q: Extend: Coeliac disease flattens villi. Explain why people with it may lose weight. [3 marks]
independent.a: Flattened villi reduce surface area (1); less absorption of digested food (1); fewer nutrients and less energy reach the body (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why the small intestine absorbs glucose by both diffusion and active transport.
independent.a: Diffusion while the gut has more glucose than the blood; active transport takes up the rest against the gradient.

exit.q: Digested food is absorbed mainly in the...
Big question: how does food get from your plate into your blood?
exit.a: It is digested into small molecules and absorbed across the villi of the small intestine into the blood.

keywords.def: reactions in cells that release energy from glucose
molecule that stores and transfers energy in cells
using oxygen
without oxygen
extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

hook.text: After a sprint you keep breathing hard for minutes even though you have stopped. Why?
hook.a: Extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration.

starter.q: Where in the cell does aerobic respiration happen?
Is respiration the same as breathing?

teach.heading: Why respire?
bullets: It transfers energy from glucose to ATP
ATP is used for movement, growth, active transport, heat
teach.note: Ask: is breathing the same as respiration? Break the misconception early. Think of ATP as the small change of the cell: glucose is the banknote, ATP the coins you can spend anywhere in the cell.

left.title: Aerobic
points: Releases a lot of energy (about 30 ATP per glucose)

right.title: Anaerobic
points: Releases far less energy (2 ATP per glucose)

teach.heading: Equations
teach.note: Compare with photosynthesis: aerobic respiration is almost the reverse. Ethanol is C₂H₅OH. Yeast fermentation makes bread rise (CO₂ bubbles) and is the basis of brewing, which pupils may meet in food science.

teach.heading: Model: oxygen debt
bullets: Say why breathing stays fast afterwards
teach.note: Elicit that lactic acid is toxic in large amounts and is broken down in the liver using oxygen. This extra oxygen is the oxygen debt.

model.problem: A sprinter breathes heavily for 5 minutes after a race. Explain why. [3 marks]
steps: During the sprint, muscles respire anaerobically as oxygen supply is too slow
After the race extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid
So breathing rate and depth stay high until it is removed
model.answer: Extra oxygen is needed to remove lactic acid built up by anaerobic respiration.

teach.heading: Practical: yeast and temperature
bullets: Yeast, glucose solution and a gas syringe
Count bubbles or measure CO₂ volume in 5 minutes
Change the temperature of the water bath
teach.note: Variables: independent is temperature (20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C); dependent is bubbles per minute; control yeast mass, glucose concentration, volume. Example mean results (bubbles per minute): 20 °C: 14; 30 °C: 32; 40 °C: 55; 50 °C: 20; 60 °C: 0. Ask pupils to explain the peak at 40 and zero at 60 (enzymes denature). Safety: hot water, goggles.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: lactic acid is the product in human muscle, not in yeast.

check.q: Which products are made when yeast respires anaerobically?
check.why: Yeast fermentation gives ethanol and carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is produced in animal muscle.

practice.q: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration. [2 marks]
practice.model:
Reactants: glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ and oxygen O₂.
Products: CO₂ and H₂O.
Balance carbon: 6CO₂.
Hydrogen: 6H₂O.
Oxygen: 6 + 12 = 18 on the right, so 6O₂ on the left (6 in glucose + 12 = 18).

practice.q: Word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast (plants).
Word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles.

independent.q: Core: Plot the yeast data (bubbles per minute against temperature) and describe the trend.
independent.a: Rises to a peak at 40 °C (55 per minute) then falls to 0 at 60 °C.
independent.model: Teacher plots 20 °C at 14 and 30 °C at 32 and describes: as temperature rises, rate increases.

independent.q: Extend: Explain the shape of the graph using enzymes. [4 marks]
independent.a: Rate rises as enzymes and substrate gain kinetic energy (1), more collisions (1); above the optimum the enzymes' active sites change shape (1), enzymes denature so rate falls to zero (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why anaerobic respiration releases less energy per glucose. [2 marks]
independent.a: Glucose is only partly broken down (1); much energy remains in lactic acid or ethanol (1).

exit.q: Products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
Big question: why do your muscles burn when you sprint, and why does bread rise?
exit.a: Muscles respire anaerobically making lactic acid; yeast respires anaerobically making carbon dioxide gas that raises dough.

teach.heading: Example results
teach.note: Discuss.

teach.heading: Carbon dioxide

teach.note: Seeds or maggots on gauze above the indicator in a sealed tube; teacher demonstration on screen.

What are the peas doing?

Energy, some as heat.

lessons.title: Relative formula mass and the mole
lessons.bigQuestion: How can chemists count atoms by weighing them?
objectives: To understand how to calculate relative formula mass and use the mole to link mass and amount
successCriteria: All: calculate Mr from Ar values

lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging and using ratios
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: precise measure in creation (al-Qamar 54:49)

keywords.def: average mass of an atom compared with carbon-12
sum of Ar values in a formula
the amount of substance containing 6 × 10²³ particles
mass of one mole, in g, equal to Mr
mass of a substance used or made in a reaction

hook.text: A dozen eggs and a dozen melons have the same number but different masses. How might chemists use a similar idea?
hook.a: A mole is a fixed number of particles; its mass depends on the substance's Mr.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, all things We created with precise measure' (al-Qamar 54:49). Chemistry's calculations rest on the fact that substances always react in fixed, measurable proportions.

teach.heading: Balanced equations
bullets: Same number of each atom on both sides
Change big numbers only, never small subscripts
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous
teach.note: Example: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Check atoms: Mg 1/1, H 2/2, Cl 2/2. Model for them: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. Ask: why can we not write FeCl₆?

teach.heading: Mr and the mole
bullets: Use Ar: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Mg 24, Ca 40
Mr = add the Ar values in the formula
teach.note: Make the idea of the mole concrete: 12 g of carbon, 18 g of water and 58.5 g of sodium chloride each contain the same number of formula units, 6.02 × 10²³ (the Avogadro constant). Show how to find Mr of Ca(OH)₂: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74.

model.problem: Calculate the Mr of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, and the moles in 25 g.

teach.heading: Reacting masses
bullets: Convert the known mass to moles
Convert moles of the unknown to mass
teach.note: Write the three-step plan on the board and have pupils use it every time. Worked: 4.8 g Mg burns. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. n(Mg) = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.20 mol. Ratio 2:2 so n(MgO) = 0.20 mol. Mr(MgO) = 40, mass = 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g. Check: the mass has increased by 3.2 g, the mass of oxygen gained.

misconception.wrong: Reacting masses are in the same ratio as the numbers in the equation.
misconception.right: The equation ratio is for moles. Convert grams to moles first, then use the ratio.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: doubling only the H (42) or only counting one OH (41). Brackets mean the whole group is doubled.

check.q: What is the Mr of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂? (Ar: Mg 24, O 16, H 1)
check.why: Mr = 24 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 58. Doubling only the H gives 42, and counting one OH gives 41.

practice.q: Calculate Mr of CaCO₃ (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16). [1 mark]
practice.model:
List atoms: 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O.
Multiply by Ar: 40 + 12 + 3 × 16.
Add: 40 + 12 + 48 = 100.

practice.q: How many moles in 88 g of CO₂?
Mass of 0.5 mol of H₂SO₄ (Mr 98)?

independent.q: Core: Calculate Mr for H₂O, NaOH, MgO, Mg(OH)₂, (NH₄)₂SO₄ and convert three given masses to moles.
independent.model: Teacher does Mg(OH)₂: 24 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 58.

independent.q: Extend: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. What mass of MgO forms from 12 g of Mg? [3 marks]
independent.a: Moles Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 (1); ratio 2:2 so 0.5 mol MgO (1); mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g (1)

independent.q: Stretch: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of CaCO₃ is needed to make 14 g of CaO?

exit.q: Moles = mass ÷ ?
Big question: how can chemists count atoms by weighing them?
exit.a: One mole of any substance has the same number of particles and a mass in grams equal to its Mr.

hook.text: Your lungs have no muscles. So how do they fill with air?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And in yourselves; then will you not see?' (adh-Dhariyat 51:21). The lungs exchange gases thousands of times a day without our thinking, a sign worth reflecting on.

Volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in

teach.heading: Alveoli
bullets: Walls one cell thick; moist lining
Surrounded by a dense capillary network
Huge surface area; ventilation keeps gradient steep
teach.note: Oxygen diffuses from alveolus to blood; carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. Blood flow carries oxygen away to keep the gradient. About 300 million alveoli per lung gives a surface area close to the size of a tennis court. Smoking: tar damages alveoli and cilia (optional).

teach.heading: Model: ventilation rate
bullets: Ventilation rate = breaths per minute × tidal volume
teach.note: Remind pupils that tidal volume is the volume per breath (about 500 cm³ at rest). Core practical idea: count breaths in 1 minute at rest, then after 2 minutes of step-ups, then time how long to return to resting rate; repeat three times.

model.problem: At rest a pupil breathes 15 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 cm³. After exercise: 28 breaths per minute, 1100 cm³. How many times greater is the ventilation rate after exercise?

teach.heading: Exhaled air test
bullets: Limewater turns milky with more CO₂
teach.note: Set up two boiler tubes of limewater with valves so that you inhale through one and exhale through the other. The exhaled-air tube goes milky faster. Safety: use clean mouthpieces; do not suck up limewater; wash hands.

misconception.wrong: We breathe out only carbon dioxide and breathe in only oxygen.
misconception.right: Inhaled air has 21% oxygen and exhaled air still has 16%; carbon dioxide rises from 0.04% to about 4%.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say pressure rises as volume rises. Air moves from high to low pressure, so pressure must fall for air to enter.

check.q: During inhalation, what happens to the pressure in the chest?
check.why: The chest volume increases so the pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in.

practice.q: Describe what happens when you breathe in. [4 marks]
practice.a: External intercostals contract, ribs up and out (1); diaphragm contracts and flattens (1); thorax volume increases (1); pressure decreases below atmospheric so air flows in (1).
practice.model:
Muscles: intercostals and diaphragm contract.
Movement: ribs up and out, diaphragm flattens.
Volume: increases.
Pressure: falls.
Air: flows in from higher pressure.

practice.q: Give three adaptations of alveoli.
practice.a: Large surface area; walls one cell thick; rich capillary network (also moist).

practice.q: Why does ventilation keep the gradient steep?
practice.a: Fresh air brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide.

independent.q: Core: Label the thorax diagram (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, ribs, intercostals, diaphragm, pleural membranes).
independent.a: Correct labels on the portal diagram.
independent.model: Teacher labels the trachea first: windpipe held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage.

independent.q: Extend (home practical, 4SD0 2.50): Count breaths per minute at rest and after 1 minute of gentle stepping. Explain the change. [3 marks]
independent.a: Rate rises (1); muscles respire faster, needing more oxygen (1) and producing more carbon dioxide to remove (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Ventilation rate = breaths per minute × tidal volume. 15 breaths, 0.5 dm³: calculate.
independent.a: 7.5 dm³ per minute

exit.q: Breathing in: thorax pressure...
Big question: how do your lungs keep your blood topped up with oxygen?
exit.a: Ventilation brings fresh air to the alveoli, which are adapted for fast diffusion into the blood.

lessons.send: SEND: labelled diagram with a word bank. EAL: ventilation, inhale, exhale. Stretch: explain why exhaled air turns limewater milky faster.

lessons.title: Smoking and the gas exchange system
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does smoking damage both the lungs and the heart?
objectives: To understand the biological effects of smoking on the lungs and circulatory system
successCriteria: All: name tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide and one effect of each
Most: explain how smoking causes bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer
Some: explain the link between smoking and coronary heart disease using data
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: health choices and addiction
lessons.smsc: Moral: Islam's teaching against harming the body

keywords.def: sticky substance in smoke that contains carcinogens
addictive drug in tobacco
gas that binds to haemoglobin
breakdown of alveolar walls, reducing surface area
narrowing of the arteries supplying the heart muscle

hook.text: Smokers often have a 'smoker's cough' first thing in the morning. What might cause it?
hook.a: Damaged cilia cannot clear mucus overnight, so it must be coughed up.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction' (al-Baqarah 2:195). Many scholars apply this to smoking, because of the harm it does to the lungs and heart that Allah entrusted to us.

starter.q: Which gas binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport?
Give one adaptation of the alveoli.
starter.a: Large surface area (thin walls, good blood supply).
Sweep mucus out of the airways.

teach.heading: What is in smoke?
teach.note: Use the table.

head: Substance
Effect
rows: addiction; narrows blood vessels; raises heart rate and blood pressure

teach.heading: Lung diseases
teach.note: Emphysema lowers surface area, so less oxygen enters the blood.

teach.heading: The heart
bullets: Nicotine and CO damage artery linings
Less oxygen to heart muscle: heart attack risk
teach.note: Link to coronary heart disease (2.67).

teach.heading: Data
teach.note: Illustrative figures based on large studies.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Emphysema reduces gas exchange because...
options: alveoli walls break down, reducing surface area
check.why: Fewer, larger air spaces give less surface area for diffusion.

practice.q: Explain why smokers become breathless. [3 marks]
practice.a: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carried (1); emphysema reduces alveolar surface area (1); so less oxygen reaches respiring cells (1).
practice.model:
Point 1: CO takes the place of oxygen on haemoglobin.
Point 2: damaged alveoli give less surface for diffusion.
Link: less oxygen reaches the muscles, so the person is breathless.

practice.q: From the chart, how many times more likely is lung cancer in someone smoking 25+ a day?
Which substance in smoke is addictive?

independent.q: Core: Make a table: substance in smoke, part of the body affected, effect, disease.
independent.a: Tar: airways, cilia, mucus, bronchitis and cancer; nicotine: heart and vessels, CHD; CO: blood, less oxygen.
independent.model: Teacher fills tar first: airways and alveoli; damages cilia and causes mutations; bronchitis and lung cancer.

independent.q: Extend: Explain how smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease. [4 marks] Use the portal response box.
independent.a: Chemicals damage the artery lining (1); fatty deposits build up, narrowing coronary arteries (1); less blood and oxygen reach heart muscle (1); risk of heart attack (1). CO and nicotine also raise heart rate and blood pressure.

independent.q: Stretch: The chart shows correlation. What other evidence shows smoking causes lung cancer?
independent.a: Tar contains carcinogens shown to cause mutations; risk falls after stopping; dose-response pattern.

exit.q: Tar in smoke can cause...
Big question: why does smoking damage both the lungs and the heart?
exit.a: Tar and particles damage airways and alveoli; nicotine and CO damage arteries and reduce oxygen supply to the heart.

lessons.title: Reacting masses and percentage yield
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do chemical factories never get 100% of the product they expect?
objectives: To understand how to calculate reacting masses and percentage yield, and why yields are below 100%
successCriteria: All: calculate percentage yield from actual and theoretical yield
Most: calculate theoretical yield from reacting masses
Some: explain reasons for low yield and calculate empirical formulae
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: efficiency and waste in manufacturing
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste of resources

keywords.def: the maximum mass of product calculated from the equation
the mass of product actually obtained
actual ÷ theoretical × 100
simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
mass of a reactant or product in a reaction

hook.text: You expected 10 g of product but collected only 8 g. Where could the other 2 g have gone?
hook.a: Lost in transfers, incomplete reaction, side reactions, or left on filter paper.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Eat and drink, but do not be wasteful' (al-A'raf 7:31). In industry, a higher yield means less waste of the resources Allah has provided.

teach.heading: Percentage yield
bullets: Yield is always below 100% in practice
Reasons: incomplete reaction, loss in transfer, side reactions
teach.note: Industry cares: low yield is wasted money and resources. Stress that you must find the theoretical yield from the equation first.

model.problem: 25.0 g of CaCO₃ is heated and 11.2 g of CaO is collected. Calculate the percentage yield. (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; Mr CaCO₃ = 100, CaO = 56)

teach.heading: Empirical formula method
bullets: Divide each mass by its Ar
Divide all by the smallest answer
Multiply to get whole numbers if needed
teach.note: Teach it as a four-column table: element, mass, moles, ratio. Example below is iron oxide; keep working visible. Ratio 0.2:0.3 gives 2:3 after multiplying by 10 (or dividing by 0.1).

model.problem: An iron oxide contains 11.2 g of iron and 4.8 g of oxygen. Find its empirical formula. (Ar: Fe 56, O 16)

teach.heading: Molecular formula
bullets: Find Mr of the empirical formula
Divide the given Mr by that
Multiply all subscripts by the result
teach.note: Examples: empirical CH₂, Mr 56; mass of CH₂ is 14; 56 ÷ 14 = 4; molecular formula C₄H₈. Percentage composition works the same way: 85.7% C and 14.3% H gives 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2, so CH₂.

teach.heading: Practical: formula of a metal oxide
bullets: Heat magnesium in a crucible with a lid
teach.note: Method: weigh empty crucible and lid; add 10 cm magnesium ribbon (coiled), weigh; heat strongly, lifting the lid briefly to let air in without letting smoke escape; cool, reweigh until constant mass. Example: Mg 0.24 g gives MgO 0.40 g, so O 0.16 g; ratio 0.01 : 0.01 gives MgO. Errors: loss of white smoke makes oxygen mass too low; incomplete burning. Safety: goggles, do not look at the bright light, use tongs. Reduction of copper(II) oxide in hydrogen is an alternative route.

misconception.wrong: The empirical formula tells you how many atoms are in one molecule.
misconception.right: It is only the simplest ratio. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in a molecule.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: using the mass ratio 6 : 1 without dividing by Ar gives C₆H.

check.q: A compound contains 6.0 g carbon and 1.0 g hydrogen. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: C 12, H 1)
check.why: C: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 mol; H: 1 ÷ 1 = 1.0 mol. Ratio 1:2, giving CH₂.

practice.q: Theoretical yield 25 g, actual 20 g. Percentage yield? [2 marks]
practice.model:
Formula: % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
Substitute: 20 ÷ 25 × 100.
Calculate: 80%.

practice.q: Give two reasons why yield is less than 100%.
practice.a: Reaction incomplete; product lost in transfer or filtering (also side reactions).

practice.q: Empirical formula of a compound with 2.4 g Mg and 1.6 g O?

independent.q: Core: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 50 g CaCO₃ is heated. Calculate the theoretical mass of CaO, then the % yield if 22.4 g is obtained.
independent.model: Teacher works the first step: moles CaCO₃ = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 mol; ratio 1:1 so 0.5 mol CaO; mass = 0.5 × 56 = 28 g.

independent.q: Extend: 4.8 g of Mg burns to give 8.0 g of oxide. Find the empirical formula. [3 marks]
independent.a: Mass of O = 3.2 g (1); moles Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2, moles O = 3.2 ÷ 16 = 0.2 (1); ratio 1:1 so MgO (1).

independent.q: Stretch: In the metal oxide practical, why is the lid lifted from time to time?
independent.a: To let oxygen in so the magnesium can react, while stopping magnesium oxide smoke escaping.

exit.q: % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × ...
Big question: why do factories never get 100% of the expected product?
exit.a: Reactions may be incomplete, product is lost during separation and transfer, and side reactions make other products.

lessons.homework: Complete the percentage yield and reacting masses question set on the portal.
lessons.send: SEND: step frame (moles, ratio, mass). EAL: yield, theoretical, actual. Stretch: molecular formula from empirical formula and Mr.

lessons.title: Series and parallel circuits
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do all the lights not go out when one bulb in your house blows?
objectives: To understand how current and voltage behave in series and parallel circuits
successCriteria: All: describe current and voltage rules in series and parallel
Most: calculate currents and voltages in simple circuits
Some: apply charge conservation at junctions to find unknown currents
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: wiring layouts
lessons.smsc: Moral: electrical safety at home

keywords.def: one path for the current
two or more branches
where a circuit splits or joins
current into a junction equals current out
one path in a parallel circuit

hook.text: Old strings of lamps all went out when one lamp failed. Modern ones do not. What changed in the wiring?
hook.a: Old ones were in series (one path); modern ones use parallel paths or bypasses.

starter.q: Total resistance of 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series?

teach.heading: Series circuits
bullets: Supply voltage is shared across components
If one component fails, all stop
teach.note: Build a series circuit from cells and bulbs. Pupils predict ammeter readings in different places. Voltmeters go in parallel with the component, ammeters in series.

model.problem: A 12 V supply is connected to a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor in series. Find the current and the voltage across each resistor.

teach.heading: Parallel circuits
bullets: Branches: voltage across each branch equals the supply
Current splits at a junction and recombines
Current into a junction = current out
teach.note: Draw the junction as a river splitting. Ask: where has the current gone? (Nowhere: charge is conserved.) The branch with lower resistance carries more current. This is why household sockets are in parallel.

model.problem: A 6.0 V supply is connected to a 12 Ω and a 6.0 Ω resistor in parallel. Find the current in each branch and the total current.

teach.heading: Charge, current and time
bullets: Current is rate of flow of charge: 1 A = 1 C per second
teach.note: Link back to the ammeter reading: an ammeter measures how much charge passes each second. Ask: how much charge passes a point at 2.5 A for 40 s?

model.problem: A current of 2.5 A flows through a lamp for 40 s. Calculate the charge that flows.

teach.heading: Series versus parallel
teach.note: Use the check as a hinge. Ask for reasons; the common error is mixing current and voltage rules.

check.q: Two identical bulbs are in parallel across a 6 V cell. What is the voltage across each bulb?
check.why: Each parallel branch has the full supply voltage of 6 V. 3 V would be the share in series.

practice.q: Two lamps in parallel on 6 V. Currents 0.4 A and 0.6 A. Supply current? Voltage across each? [2 marks]
practice.model:
Parallel: currents in branches add: 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.0 A.
Voltage across each branch equals the supply: 6 V.

practice.q: In series, the supply is 9 V and one lamp has 4 V. The other?
In series, the current is 0.3 A at one point. Elsewhere?

independent.q: Core: Six circuit diagrams (portal worksheet): find the missing currents and voltages.
independent.a: Answers in the key, e.g. junction: 1.5 A in, 0.5 A in one branch, 1.0 A in the other.
independent.model: Teacher solves diagram 1: series with 12 V supply and 3 V across lamp A: lamp B has 9 V; same current everywhere.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why homes use parallel circuits for lighting. [3 marks]
independent.a: Each lamp gets the full supply voltage (1); each can be switched independently (1); if one fails the others still work (1).

independent.q: Stretch: Three identical lamps in parallel on 12 V draw 1.5 A in total. Current in each, and resistance of each?

exit.q: In parallel, the voltage across each branch...
Big question: why do the other lights stay on when one bulb blows?
exit.a: Household lighting is in parallel: each lamp is on its own branch.

lessons.homework: Complete the series and parallel question set on the portal.
lessons.send: SEND: rule card (series and parallel). EAL: branch, junction, series, parallel. Stretch: explain why adding branches lowers total resistance.

lessons.title: Why homes use parallel circuits, and how resistance changes the current
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to the current from the supply when you switch on more appliances?
objectives: To understand why domestic circuits are wired in parallel and how resistance affects current
successCriteria: All: give two advantages of parallel wiring at home
Most: explain why supply current rises as branches are added
Some: explain why overloading a socket is dangerous
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: adding currents and using I = V ÷ R
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding overloaded sockets protects the family

keywords.def: the wiring in a home
too much current drawn from one circuit or socket
total current from the supply
a wire that melts if the current is too high
one path in a parallel circuit

hook.text: Plugging a kettle, heater and toaster into one extension lead can make it hot. Why?
hook.a: Each adds a branch, so the total current through the lead rises and heats its wires.

starter.a: Melts to break the circuit if current is too high.

teach.heading: Series versus parallel
bullets: Series: one path; all stop if one breaks
Series: voltage is shared between components
Parallel: each branch has the full supply voltage
Parallel: other branches work if one breaks
teach.note: Use a string-of-fairy-lights example: older series sets went out entirely when one bulb failed. Mains lighting uses parallel branches so each lamp has 230 V, can be switched independently, and has full brightness. Series is useful when you want a component to work only if all conditions are met (e.g. a safety interlock where all switches must be closed).

teach.heading: Resistance and current
bullets: At a fixed voltage, more resistance means less current
A variable resistor dims or brightens a lamp
A thermistor or LDR changes resistance with conditions
teach.note: Link the qualitative idea to the formula: double the resistance and the current halves for a fixed voltage. A variable resistor in series with a lamp: increasing its resistance reduces current, dimming the lamp. Adding resistors in series increases total resistance and lowers current; adding in parallel provides extra paths so total resistance falls and the supply current rises.

model.problem: A 12 V supply is connected to a 6.0 ohm resistor and then to a 12 ohm resistor. Calculate the current each time and describe the pattern.
steps: Doubling the resistance halved the current
model.answer: 2.0 A then 1.0 A: more resistance, less current.

teach.heading: Check: parallel branches
teach.note: Option B comes from thinking the cell voltage is shared in parallel. D confuses current with voltage.

check.q: Three identical lamps are connected in parallel to a 6 V cell. What is the voltage across each lamp?
check.why: Each branch of a parallel circuit has the full cell voltage, so 6 V.

teach.heading: Why does the supply current rise?
bullets: Total resistance of parallel branches falls
Supply current is the sum of the branch currents
So too many appliances on one socket is dangerous
teach.note: Ask: what happens if many appliances are plugged into one extension lead? The currents add, so the cable overheats, which is why fuses are used and why we avoid overloading sockets. Link to earlier mains safety lessons.

practice.q: A kettle (13 A), toaster (4 A) and lamp (0.5 A) run from one lead. Total current? [1 mark]
practice.model:
Parallel branches: add the currents.
13 + 4 + 0.5 = 17.5 A.
A 13 A extension lead would be overloaded.

practice.q: Why is this dangerous?
practice.a: The current exceeds the lead's rating, so wires overheat and could start a fire.

practice.q: Adding branches makes total resistance...

independent.q: Core: Calculate the current for six appliances at 230 V from their resistances (portal worksheet) and the total if all run together.
independent.a: Answers in the key, e.g. 23 Ω heater: 10 A.
independent.model: Teacher does the first: lamp 920 Ω: I = 230 ÷ 920 = 0.25 A.

independent.q: Extend: Explain, using resistance, why adding branches increases supply current. [3 marks]
independent.a: Each branch gives another path (1); total resistance decreases (1); for the same voltage, I = V ÷ R so current increases (1).

independent.q: Stretch: With an adult, list the appliances on one extension lead at home and check the total current against its rating (look at labels only).
independent.a: Pupils' own; total should stay below 13 A.

exit.q: More appliances on in parallel means supply current...
Big question: what happens to the supply current when you switch on more appliances?
exit.a: It increases because each adds a branch and total resistance falls.

lessons.homework: Write a short safety guide for your family about extension leads using the science from this lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: addition grid for branch currents. EAL: overload, extension lead, rating. Stretch: link to fuse ratings and P = IV next term.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The heart, blood vessels and coronary heart disease
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a blocked artery as small as a pencil lead stop the heart?
objectives: Describe the structure of the heart and double circulation
Compare arteries, veins and capillaries
Explain the causes and risk factors of coronary heart disease
successCriteria: All: label the heart and name the vessels
Most: link vessel structure to function
Some: explain coronary heart disease and evaluate risk factors
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: exercise and heart rate; Maths: rates
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for health; moderation (wasatiyyah) in diet and lifestyle

keywords.def: blood passes through the heart twice on each complete circuit
vessel carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure
vessel carrying blood towards the heart; has valves
artery supplying the heart muscle with oxygenated blood

starter: Bismillah. Which blood component carries oxygen?
Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
What does the diaphragm do in inhalation?

teach.heading: The heart and double circulation
bullets: Right side: deoxygenated blood to the lungs
Left side: oxygenated blood to the body
Valves stop backflow; left ventricle wall is thickest
teach.note: Trace one drop of blood: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta. Show a labelled diagram. Heart rate rises with exercise because adrenaline and the brain signal the heart.
cycle: Vena cava brings blood from the body
Pulmonary vein returns to left atrium
Left ventricle pumps blood out through the aorta

teach.heading: Three kinds of vessel
bullets: Arteries: thick, muscular, elastic walls; narrow lumen
Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves
Capillaries: one cell thick for exchange
teach.note: Pupils often say all arteries carry oxygenated blood. Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

teach.heading: Model: structure to function
bullets: Name the feature, the function, then the link
teach.note: Practice phrasing: the left ventricle pumps to the whole body, the right only to the lungs next door.

model.problem: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the right. [2 marks]
steps: The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, a long way
This needs a higher pressure than pumping to the nearby lungs
A thicker muscular wall contracts more strongly to give that pressure
model.answer: A thicker wall generates the greater pressure needed to pump blood around the body.

teach.heading: Coronary heart disease
bullets: Less oxygen reaches heart muscle: chest pain, heart attack
Risk: diet high in saturated fat, smoking, stress, genetics
teach.note: Distinguish risk factors that can be changed (diet, smoking, exercise, stress) from those that cannot (genes, age, sex). Explain that correlation shows association, not proof of cause; link to evaluating data in exam questions.

misconception.wrong: Veins carry deoxygenated blood and arteries carry oxygenated blood, always.
misconception.right: Direction relative to the heart defines them. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer D. Trap: the rule 'arteries carry oxygenated blood' leads pupils to pick the pulmonary artery.

check.q: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
check.why: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

practice: List the heart chambers in the order blood flows through them.
State two adaptations of veins.
Why does the heart muscle need its own blood supply?
independent: Core: Compare the structure of an artery and a vein.
Extend: Heart rate was 68 beats per minute at rest and 142 after exercise. Calculate the percentage increase. [2 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the claim that stress alone causes coronary heart disease. [4 marks]
exit: Describe what happens in the coronary arteries in coronary heart disease. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: link a narrow artery to oxygen and heart muscle.
lessons.homework: Draw a flow diagram of double circulation using two colours for oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded diagram. Stretch: how do stents and statins reduce risk?
