lessons.title: Static electricity: charging by friction, uses and dangers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a balloon rubbed on a jumper stick to a wall?
objectives: Explain charging by friction using electron transfer
Describe attraction and repulsion between charges
Describe uses and dangers of static electricity
successCriteria: All: state that like charges repel and unlike attract
Most: explain how an insulator becomes charged by rubbing
Some: explain an application or danger of static in detail, including earthing
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: atoms and electrons; Geography: lightning
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at natural forces such as lightning, and humility before them

keywords.def: charge that builds up on an insulator and stays there
rubbing, which can transfer electrons between surfaces
a material that does not let charge flow through it
connecting a charged object to the ground so charge flows away

starter: Bismillah. State the charge on a proton, neutron and electron.
Which particles move when current flows in a metal wire?
Give one use of an insulator.

teach.heading: Charging by friction
bullets: Rubbing transfers electrons from one insulator to another
The surface that gains electrons becomes negative
The surface that loses electrons becomes positive
teach.note: Demonstrate with a polythene rod and cloth, using a hanging charged rod and a paper strip. Ask which gains electrons for polythene rubbed with a cloth: the rod gains electrons (negative), the cloth loses them (positive). Both end up with equal and opposite charges.

model.problem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. Explain how.
steps: Both begin with equal positive and negative charges
Friction transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod
The rod has gained extra electrons so has a negative charge
The cloth has lost electrons so is positively charged
model.answer: Electrons move from the cloth to the rod; the rod is negative and the cloth positive

teach.heading: Forces between charges
bullets: A charged insulator attracts small neutral objects
The force is greater when the charges are closer
teach.note: Show two hanging charged rods repelling and a rod with a cloth attracting. Explain how a charged object attracts neutral paper: charges in the paper redistribute, so the near side has opposite charge and is attracted.

check.q: Two negatively charged balloons are brought close together. What happens?
check.why: Like charges repel. Option A is unlike charges; C and D are not correct because both carry negative charge.

teach.heading: Uses of static
bullets: Electrostatic spraying: paint droplets repel and coat evenly
Electrostatic precipitators remove smoke particles in chimneys
Photocopiers and laser printers use charged drums
teach.note: Explain the spray gun: the droplets all gain the same charge so repel and spread evenly; the object is oppositely charged or earthed so attracts the paint, wrapping around the back. This is a typical exam scenario.

head: Use
How it works
rows: droplets charged by the gun repel; attracted to earthed object
charged plates attract charged smoke particles
charged drum attracts oppositely charged toner

teach.heading: Dangers and earthing
bullets: Sparks can ignite fuel vapour or flammable gases
Aircraft and tankers are earthed when refuelling
Earthing lets charge flow safely to the ground
teach.note: Explain how a fuel tanker is earthed to stop a spark. Also clothes crackling and small shocks from car doors. Remind pupils that the safest response to lightning is to shelter, not stand under tall trees, which is common-sense safety.

misconception.wrong: Charging by friction creates new charge from nothing.
misconception.right: Charge is not created. Electrons are transferred from one object to another, so total charge stays the same.

practice: Describe how a balloon becomes charged when rubbed on hair.
Explain why car refuelling hoses are earthed.
A positively charged rod is brought near a hanging negatively charged ball. State what happens and why.
independent: Core: Explain how an electrostatic precipitator removes smoke particles.
Extend: A rod charged negatively touches an uncharged metal sphere on an insulating stand. Describe what happens to the electrons and the final charge on the sphere.
Stretch: Explain, in terms of charge movement, why a charged plastic comb picks up small pieces of neutral paper.
exit: State which particle is transferred when an insulator is charged by friction.
Give one use and one danger of static electricity.
lessons.homework: Research one real application of static electricity and write a paragraph explaining how charge makes it work.
lessons.send: SEND: step cards for electron transfer with drawings. EAL: pre-teach attract, repel, discharge. Stretch: explain charging by induction using an earthed sphere.

lessons.title: Sound waves: hearing range, speed of sound, pitch and loudness
lessons.bigQuestion: How can an oscilloscope help us see the difference between a quiet low note and a loud high note?
objectives: Describe sound as a longitudinal wave needing a medium
State the human hearing range and typical speeds of sound
Interpret oscilloscope traces for pitch and loudness
successCriteria: All: state the range of human hearing and that sound needs a medium
Most: calculate distance using the speed of sound and echoes
Some: calculate frequency from an oscilloscope trace and design a speed-of-sound experiment
lessons.crossCurricular: Health: hearing, pitch and loudness; Maths: speed = distance ÷ time
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the beauty of sound in recitation and the care taken to protect our hearing

keywords.def: region where the air particles are close together, high pressure
region where particles are spread out, low pressure
sound above 20 000 Hz
how high or low a note sounds: depends on frequency

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the speed of a wave with f = 250 Hz and λ = 1.36 m.
Is sound longitudinal or transverse?
Convert 20 kHz to Hz.

teach.heading: How sound travels
bullets: Source vibrates and pushes particles: compressions and rarefactions
Needs a medium: no sound in a vacuum
Faster in solids than liquids than gases
Human hearing: about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
teach.note: Bell jar demonstration: sound fades as air is removed. Particles are closer in solids so vibrations pass more quickly. Typical speeds: air about 340 m/s, water about 1500 m/s, steel about 5000 m/s.

teach.heading: Echoes and the speed of sound
bullets: d = v × t, but the sound travels there and back
Distance to the wall = ½ × v × t
teach.note: Practical idea: two pupils stand 100 m from a large wall; one claps, the other starts a stopwatch on each echo, timing 20 echoes to reduce error. Alternatively use two microphones connected to a timer. Safety: keep away from roads. Use the 340 m/s value unless the question gives another.

model.problem: A pupil claps and hears the echo from a cliff 0.50 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
steps: Distance there and back = v × t = 340 × 0.50 = 170 m

teach.heading: Pitch and loudness on an oscilloscope
bullets: Higher pitch means higher frequency: more waves on the screen
Louder means larger amplitude: taller waves
Period from the time base: T = divisions × time per division
teach.note: Show traces of a quiet low note, a loud low note and a quiet high note. The vertical axis shows voltage (amplitude), the horizontal shows time. Read off the time for one complete wave.

model.problem: On an oscilloscope, one complete wave takes 4.0 divisions. The time base is set to 2.5 ms per division. Calculate the frequency.

teach.heading: Check: trace comparison
teach.note: Option A reverses amplitude and frequency. Ask pupils which feature of the trace is the pitch and which is the loudness.

check.q: Trace B has the same height as trace A but twice as many waves across the screen. Compared with A, the sound in B is...
options: the same loudness and higher pitched
the same loudness and lower pitched
check.why: Same height means the same amplitude, so the same loudness. More waves in the same time means a higher frequency, so a higher pitch.

practice: Calculate the wavelength of a 400 Hz note in air, speed 340 m/s.
A ship's sonar sends a pulse and detects the echo from the sea bed after 0.80 s. The speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth.
A trace has a period of 5.0 ms. Calculate the frequency.
independent: Core: State two differences between a loud, low-pitched sound and a quiet, high-pitched sound.
Extend: Lightning is seen, and thunder heard 6.0 s later. Estimate the distance to the lightning (speed of sound 340 m/s).
Stretch: Design an experiment to measure the speed of sound in air, listing the equipment, measurements, calculation and one way to reduce uncertainty.
exit: State the range of human hearing.
Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
lessons.homework: Write a short explanation of why a space film showing explosions with sound is not realistic, using the idea of a medium.
lessons.send: SEND: give an oscilloscope grid with annotated example traces. EAL: pre-teach amplitude, pitch, echo. Stretch: explain why sound speeds differ in terms of particle spacing.

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Energy stores, transfers, conservation and efficiency
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the energy go when a light bulb is switched on, and can it ever be destroyed?
objectives: Describe energy stores and transfers
State the principle of conservation of energy
Calculate efficiency and interpret Sankey diagrams
successCriteria: All: name energy stores and transfers in a system
Most: calculate efficiency
Some: draw and interpret a Sankey diagram with correct arrow widths
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: energy changes; Maths: percentages and ratios
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste (israf) of resources, including energy

keywords.def: a way energy is kept, such as chemical, kinetic or gravitational potential
energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or dissipated
useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100%)
spread out to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the power of a device transferring 600 J in 20 s.
Name two renewable and two non-renewable energy resources.
Calculate 18 as a percentage of 24.

teach.heading: Stores and transfers
bullets: Stores: chemical, kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, nuclear
Transfers: mechanical work, electrical work, heating, radiation (light, sound)
teach.note: Describe a few systems on the board: a boiling kettle, a falling ball, a speaker. Ask pupils to name the stores and transfers. Energy is conserved, but much becomes less useful thermal energy in the surroundings.

teach.heading: Efficiency
bullets: Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input
teach.note: Say clearly that energy is not 'lost'; it dissipates. Efficiency may also be written using power: useful power output ÷ total power input. Do a quick check: can a device be 120% efficient?

model.problem: A motor takes in 200 J of electrical energy and lifts a load, gaining 150 J of gravitational potential energy. Calculate its efficiency and the energy wasted.

teach.heading: Sankey diagrams
bullets: Arrow width shows the amount of energy
Input arrow splits into useful and wasted arrows
The widths add up to the input
Use a scale, e.g. 1 mm = 1 J
teach.note: Draw a Sankey for a 100 J lamp: 10 J light and 90 J thermal. Ask pupils to draw the arrow widths to scale on squared paper. The input arrow and the output arrows must balance.

model.problem: A kettle transfers 2000 J of electrical energy. 1800 J heats the water and 200 J heats the surroundings. Describe the Sankey diagram and calculate the efficiency.
steps: Input arrow: width 20 mm (1 mm = 100 J)
Useful arrow: width 18 mm (heating the water)

teach.heading: Check: efficiency
teach.note: Option A uses the wasted fraction. Option D is an impossible value. Ask how to check the answer is sensible.

check.q: A device wastes 30 J of every 120 J supplied. Its efficiency is...
check.why: Useful output = 120 - 30 = 90 J, so efficiency = 90 ÷ 120 = 75%. 25% is the wasted fraction.

practice: A lamp takes in 60 J and gives out 6 J of light. Calculate its efficiency and the wasted energy.
Name the energy stores before and after a ball is dropped and hits the floor.
Draw a Sankey diagram for a 400 J input with 300 J useful output.
independent: Core: A toaster transfers 1000 J electrically: 800 J heats the bread. Calculate the efficiency.
Extend: A machine is 40% efficient and wastes 90 J. Calculate the input energy.
Stretch: Two light bulbs give the same light. Bulb A has efficiency 8% and bulb B 40%. Compare the energy input needed from each to produce 20 J of light.
exit: State the principle of conservation of energy.
A motor has an efficiency of 60%. Calculate its useful output if the input is 500 J.
lessons.homework: Choose two household devices, identify the energy transfers and draw a Sankey diagram for each using realistic percentages.
lessons.send: SEND: give squared-paper Sankey templates with scales. EAL: pre-teach waste, dissipate, efficient. Stretch: efficiency of energy chains such as power stations.

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Thermal energy transfer: conduction, convection and radiation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a vacuum flask keep tea hot for hours?
objectives: Describe conduction, convection and radiation
Explain how to reduce unwanted thermal transfer
Plan an investigation of heat transfer using cooling
successCriteria: All: name the three methods of thermal transfer
Most: explain each in terms of particles or waves
Some: explain how a design reduces all three and plan a fair test
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: insulation; Geography: weather
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the environment through reducing energy waste in homes

keywords.def: transfer of thermal energy through a solid by vibrating particles and free electrons
transfer of thermal energy by the movement of a heated fluid
transfer of thermal energy as infrared waves, needing no medium
a material that is a poor conductor of thermal energy

starter: Bismillah. State two ways to improve the efficiency of a device.
Calculate the efficiency when 45 J of 60 J is useful.
State the speed of infrared radiation in a vacuum.

teach.heading: Conduction
bullets: In solids, particles vibrate and pass energy on
Metals conduct best: free electrons carry energy quickly
Trapped air is a good insulator
teach.note: Demonstrate with metal rods coated in wax, heated at one end. Link to why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one at the same temperature: it conducts heat away from your hand faster.

teach.heading: Convection and radiation
bullets: Convection: hot fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser fluid sinks, setting up a convection current
Dark matt surfaces absorb and emit best; shiny surfaces are poor
teach.note: Show a convection current with potassium permanganate crystals in water over a heat source, or a heater in a room. For radiation ask how the Sun's energy reaches us: through a vacuum, so it is not conduction or convection.
cycle: Fluid is heated at the bottom
It expands and becomes less dense
It cools at the top, becomes denser and sinks
The cycle continues as a convection current

teach.heading: Core practical idea: surfaces and cooling
bullets: Four identical cans: matt black, shiny silver, white, and shiny with a lid
Fill each with the same volume of hot water
Record the temperature every minute for 10 minutes
Plot temperature against time for each can
teach.note: Independent variable: surface colour or finish; dependent: temperature fall over 10 min; controls: starting temperature, volume of water, room, thermometer. Expected result: the matt black can cools fastest as it emits the most radiation. Safety: hot water, scald risk; use a kettle with care and keep spills away from sockets.

model.problem: Explain how a vacuum flask reduces heat loss by conduction, convection and radiation.
steps: Vacuum between the walls: no particles, so no conduction or convection
Silvered (shiny) surfaces: reflect infrared radiation back
Plastic stopper: poor conductor and traps air to reduce convection
Result: the tea stays hot for a long time
model.answer: The flask reduces all three methods of transfer

teach.heading: Reducing unwanted transfers at home
bullets: Loft insulation: traps air, reduces conduction and convection
Cavity wall insulation: stops convection in the gap
Double glazing: trapped air or vacuum reduces conduction
Reflective foil behind radiators reflects radiation
teach.note: Link back to energy efficiency. Ask pupils which measure would be most cost-effective and why: payback time = cost ÷ yearly saving. Check the hinge question on the next section.

check.q: Why is a layer of trapped air a good insulator?
options: Air is a good conductor and convection stops
Air is a poor conductor and cannot circulate easily when trapped
Air is lighter than most solids
check.why: Air is a poor conductor, and in small trapped pockets it cannot form convection currents. The other statements are not the reason.

practice: Explain why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature.
State how thermal energy from the Sun reaches the Earth.
Explain why the cooling coil of a fridge is at the back and painted black.
independent: Core: Describe how a convection current forms in a pan of water heated from below.
Extend: A householder installs loft insulation costing £400, saving £80 per year. Calculate the payback time and comment on its value.
Stretch: Explain, with reference to particles and electrons, why copper is a better conductor than glass.
exit: Name the three methods of thermal energy transfer.
Explain why shiny surfaces are used on vacuum flasks.
lessons.homework: Design a fair test to compare two different insulating materials around a beaker of hot water. State the variables, equipment and a safety point.
lessons.send: SEND: give a table to complete: method / medium needed / example. EAL: pre-teach insulate, current, trap. Stretch: investigate rate of cooling and Newton's law of cooling qualitatively.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Work done, gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy
lessons.bigQuestion: How much energy does it take to climb a hill, and where does it go when you roll down?
objectives: Calculate work done using W = Fd
Calculate gravitational potential and kinetic energy
Use conservation of energy to find speed or height
successCriteria: All: use W = Fd
Most: use ΔGPE = mgh and KE = ½mv²
Some: combine GPE and KE in conservation problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: squaring and square roots; PE: energy in sport
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: observing how effort transfers energy

keywords.def: energy transferred when a force moves an object, W = F × d
energy stored in an object due to its height, mgh
energy of a moving object, ½mv²
the unit of energy and work: 1 N m

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the weight of a 5.0 kg bag (g = 10 N/kg).
Calculate the efficiency when 80 J of 200 J is useful.
State the unit of energy.

teach.heading: Work done
bullets: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force
Work done equals the energy transferred
teach.note: Link to energy transfer: pushing a box increases its kinetic energy or heats surfaces through friction. A common error is using the wrong distance, or a force at 90° to the motion that does no work.

model.problem: A man pushes a box with a force of 50 N for 4.0 m across the floor. Calculate the work done.

teach.heading: Gravitational potential energy
bullets: Change in GPE when lifted through height h
g = 10 N/kg unless the question gives a different value
teach.note: Lifting a mass needs a force equal to its weight, so work done = mg × h. That is the link between work and GPE. Use a ball lifted onto a table as a visual.

model.problem: A 60 kg climber ascends a 3.0 m wall. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy.

teach.heading: Kinetic energy
bullets: Speed is squared: double the speed means four times the KE
Energy in joules, mass in kg, speed in m/s
teach.note: Insist on squaring v before multiplying. Ask pupils: why is speed so important in crash energy? Link to Physics 1 stopping distances.

model.problem: A 1200 kg car travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

teach.heading: Energy conservation: falling objects
bullets: A falling object transfers GPE to KE
If drag is ignored: mgh = ½mv²
teach.note: Do the example and ask: would a heavier ball land faster in a vacuum? (No, mass cancels.) Remind pupils that with air resistance some energy becomes thermal.

model.problem: A ball is dropped from rest from 5.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before hitting the ground.
steps: GPE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv²

teach.heading: Check: kinetic energy
teach.note: Option A is the common error of doubling KE when speed doubles. Ask pupils to calculate to check.

check.q: A cyclist doubles her speed. Her kinetic energy becomes...
check.why: KE depends on v², so doubling the speed gives 2² = 4 times the KE.

practice: Calculate the work done by a 15 N force moving an object 6.0 m.
Calculate the KE of a 0.50 kg ball moving at 12 m/s.
A 2.0 kg book is lifted 1.5 m. Calculate the gain in GPE.
independent: Core: A 70 kg person climbs 20 stairs of height 0.18 m each. Calculate the work done against gravity.
Extend: A 0.20 kg ball is thrown upwards at 15 m/s. Calculate the maximum height, ignoring air resistance.
Stretch: A 1000 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to rest using a constant 5000 N braking force. Calculate the braking distance and discuss what happens to the energy.
exit: State the equation for kinetic energy.
Calculate the work done when a 40 N force moves a trolley 3.0 m.
lessons.homework: Complete a table of five energy calculations (work, GPE, KE) with units and write one sentence on where the energy goes in each.
lessons.send: SEND: use a formula triangle card and a squared number reminder. EAL: pre-teach gravitational, kinetic. Stretch: explain why braking distance is proportional to v².
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Power as the rate of energy transfer
lessons.bigQuestion: Two students climb the same stairs; why can one of them be more powerful?
objectives: Define power as the rate of doing work or transferring energy
Use P = W ÷ t and P = E ÷ t
Plan an experiment to measure the power of a person climbing stairs
successCriteria: All: use P = E ÷ t
Most: combine W = Fd or mgh with power
Some: plan a stair-climb power investigation and evaluate it
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: fitness and performance; Maths: rearranging
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest measurement, working with a partner safely

keywords.def: the rate of transferring energy or doing work, in watts
one joule per second
energy transferred by a force over a distance
how much per unit of time

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the GPE of a 50 kg student on a 4.0 m balcony.
Calculate the work done when 20 N moves an object 5.0 m.
Convert 3 kW to W.

teach.heading: Power
bullets: P = W ÷ t or P = E ÷ t
A more powerful device transfers energy faster
teach.note: Compare two motors lifting the same load: both do the same work, but the more powerful one does it in less time. Link to power ratings on appliances (P = IV).

model.problem: A motor lifts a 20 kg load through 2.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the power. (g = 10 N/kg)

teach.heading: Power and efficiency
bullets: Useful power output ÷ total power input
teach.note: Remind pupils that efficiency compares powers equally well because time cancels. A 500 W motor that gives 350 W of useful output is 70% efficient.

model.problem: A pump has an input power of 800 W and lifts water, gaining GPE at 600 J every second. Calculate its efficiency and the wasted power.

teach.heading: Core practical idea: your power on the stairs
bullets: Measure your mass and the vertical height of the stairs
Time how long you take to climb them
teach.note: Variables: independent: speed of climbing or person; dependent: power; control: same stairs. Measure height with a metre rule or from step height × number of steps. Take repeats. Safety: do not run on stairs; stop if breathless. Expect 150 to 300 W for a short climb. Discuss errors: reaction time, not exact vertical height.

model.problem: A 55 kg student climbs stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 5.0 s. Calculate the power.

teach.heading: Check: power calculation
teach.note: Option A divides the wrong way round. Option C forgets time. Ask for units.

check.q: A machine does 600 J of work in 15 s. Its power is...
check.why: P = W ÷ t = 600 ÷ 15 = 40 W. 9000 comes from multiplying; 0.025 from inverting.

practice: Calculate the power of a crane that lifts a 500 N load through 6.0 m in 10 s.
A 2.0 kW heater runs for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
A motor transfers 3000 J in 20 s. Calculate its power.
independent: Core: Write a method to measure the power of a student climbing stairs, with the equipment and the calculation.
Extend: A 60 W lamp is 5% efficient. Calculate the useful light power and the thermal power.
Stretch: A 1500 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate the average useful power.
exit: State the unit of power and what it means.
A 3.0 kW kettle runs for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
lessons.homework: Measure your own stair-climb power at home (with a safe set of stairs) and write up the method, results and one improvement.
lessons.send: SEND: use a three-row table: work, time, power. EAL: pre-teach rate, per second. Stretch: compare maximum human power with machines.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Generating electricity: fuels, nuclear and renewable resources
lessons.bigQuestion: Which energy sources should a country use to keep the lights on for the next fifty years?
objectives: Describe how electricity is generated in power stations
Compare renewable and non-renewable resources
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of each resource
successCriteria: All: describe a basic power station and name sources
Most: give an advantage and a disadvantage for each source
Some: evaluate a choice of resource for a given location
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: energy supply and sustainability; Citizenship: environmental policy
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship (khalifah) of the Earth and fairness to future generations

keywords.def: a resource that is replaced as fast as it is used, or will not run out
a resource that will run out, such as coal, oil, gas and uranium
a device that transfers kinetic energy to electrical energy
a rotor turned by steam, wind or water

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the efficiency when 90 J of 360 J is useful.
State the energy transfer in a wind turbine.
State what is meant by a fossil fuel.

teach.heading: How most power stations work
bullets: Fuel releases thermal energy (burning or nuclear fission)
Turbine spins a generator, producing electricity
teach.note: Draw the energy chain. Note that wind, water and tidal power skip the boiler and drive the turbine directly; solar cells produce electricity directly. Geothermal uses hot rocks to make steam.
cycle: Chemical or nuclear energy released as thermal energy

teach.heading: Comparing the resources
bullets: Fossil fuels: reliable but release CO₂ and are finite
Nuclear: no CO₂, but produces radioactive waste
Wind, solar, hydro, tidal, geothermal: renewable, no fuel cost
Intermittent supply is a limit for wind and solar
teach.note: Pupils annotate the table with one extra point each from memory, for example wind: no fuel; visual impact; works only when the wind blows. Ask which sources can be switched on quickly to meet demand. Gas and hydro are quick.

head: Source
Advantage
Disadvantage
rows: no CO₂, small amount of fuel
depends on wind, visual and noise impact
only by day, high initial cost

teach.heading: Evaluating a choice
bullets: Weigh them up and reach a judgement
Use evidence: reliability, cost, pollution, location
teach.note: Use the model as a template for 6-mark answers. Pupils should use connecting words (however, therefore). Do not push a particular view; teach the structure of an evaluation.

model.problem: A remote island needs electricity. Evaluate using wind turbines compared with a diesel generator.
steps: Wind: renewable, no fuel deliveries and no CO₂
Wind: variable supply, needs backup or storage
Diesel: reliable on demand but fuel must be shipped; CO₂ and noise
Judgement: combine wind with storage or a small diesel generator for reliability
model.answer: A mix of wind with backup is likely best: it cuts fuel use but still gives a reliable supply

teach.heading: Check: renewable
teach.note: Option B is a typical error (nuclear fuel is not replaced). Ask why 'renewable' does not mean 'no disadvantage'.

check.q: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
check.why: Tidal energy is replenished by the Moon's pull and the Sun. Uranium, gas and coal are finite.

practice: Describe how a coal-fired power station produces electricity.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of nuclear power.
Explain why solar cells are not suitable as the only source of electricity for a UK city.
independent: Core: Make a table of three renewable and three non-renewable resources with one advantage each.
Extend: Explain why hydroelectric power can respond more quickly to demand than coal.
Stretch: Evaluate whether a country with high sun and little rain should invest in solar farms or in importing gas, giving a reasoned conclusion.
exit: State what is meant by a renewable resource.
Explain why a wind farm may not always provide electricity.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark evaluation: 'Should the UK build more nuclear power stations or more wind farms?' using the structure from the lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: give the energy chain cards to order and annotate. EAL: pre-teach renewable, finite, generate. Stretch: discuss grid storage and demand management.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Practical: food tests and the energy in food
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you prove what is in a biscuit, and how much energy it holds, without tasting it?
objectives: Carry out and interpret the tests for glucose, starch, protein and fat
Describe the practical to find the energy content of a food sample (Higher/Paper 2 only)
Calculate energy per gram from a temperature rise
successCriteria: All: state the reagent and positive colour for each of the four food tests
Most: plan a safe, fair test and explain a result
Some: calculate energy per gram and evaluate the error (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: colour changes and specific heat capacity; Maths: rearranging equations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude (shukr) for provision and care in what we eat

keywords.def: a sugar such as glucose that gives a colour change with Benedict's solution
blue solution that turns purple or lilac with protein
ethanol then water: a cloudy white layer shows lipid (fat)
measuring energy released by burning a fuel or food using the heating of water

starter: Name the elements in a carbohydrate and in a protein.
Name the basic units that make up a protein.
What does an iodine solution look like at the start?

teach.heading: Four tests, four results
bullets: Test each sample in a clean tube
Heat only the Benedict's tube, in a water bath
teach.note: Display the table and let pupils cover the right-hand column and recall it. Benedict's needs a hot water bath (about 80 degrees C), not direct flame. Goggles on for all four tests.

head: Nutrient
Reagent
Method
Positive result
rows: Blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red
Shake with ethanol, pour into water

teach.heading: Model: interpret a set of results
bullets: Use the colour to judge what is present
More colour change means more sugar
Always compare with a negative control
teach.note: Talk through each step aloud. Stress that Benedict's gives a semi-quantitative idea only (green means a little, brick-red a lot).

model.problem: A food extract turns brick-red with Benedict's, blue-black with iodine and stays blue with biuret. The ethanol test gives a clear solution. What does it contain?
steps: Brick-red Benedict's means a lot of reducing sugar such as glucose
Blue-black iodine means starch is present
Biuret stayed blue so there is no protein
A clear ethanol test means no fat
model.answer: Glucose and starch present; no protein and no fat

teach.heading: Check: choose the test
bullets: Pick the test and the result
teach.note: Hinge question. Most pupils choose the iodine option; discuss why heating is wrong for it.

check.q: A student adds iodine solution to a potato extract. Which result shows starch is present?
check.why: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. Brick-red is Benedict's with a lot of glucose, purple is biuret with protein, and a cloudy white layer is the lipid emulsion test.

teach.heading: Energy content of food (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Burn a weighed sample under a boiling tube of water
Measure the water temperature before and after
Energy = water mass x 4.2 x temperature rise
Divide by food mass for energy per gram
teach.note: Flag clearly: this point is Higher/Paper 2 only. Specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J per g per degree C. 1 cm3 of water has a mass of 1 g. Safety: tie back hair, keep nuts away from anyone with allergies, use tongs or a mounted needle.

teach.heading: Model: calculate energy per gram (Higher/Paper 2 only)
teach.note: Do the three-line calculation on the board; then ask why the real value in a data book is higher.

model.problem: 20 g of water is heated by 18 degrees C when 0.50 g of a nut burns. Calculate the energy released per gram of nut (4.2 J per g per degree C).
steps: Energy to water = 20 x 4.2 x 18 = 1512 J
Energy per gram = 1512 / 0.50 = 3024 J per g
Convert: 3024 J per g = about 3.0 kJ per g
model.answer: About 3.0 kJ per g (3024 J per g)

teach.heading: Why is the answer too low?
bullets: Some energy heats the tube and stand
teach.note: Improvements: draught shield or foil, put the tube close to the flame, stir the water, insulate. Ask pupils to say which fix tackles which loss.

misconception.wrong: The temperature rise measures all the energy in the food
misconception.right: Only part of the energy reaches the water, so the result underestimates the true value

practice: State the positive result for the biuret test.
A sample gives no colour change with Benedict's after heating. What does this tell you?
Higher: 25 g of water rises by 12 degrees C when 0.75 g of food burns. Calculate energy per gram.
independent: Core: Complete a results table of the four tests for milk, bread, egg white and oil with predictions.
Extend: Write a method to find which of three crisps has the most energy, listing control variables.
Stretch (Higher/Paper 2 only): Evaluate the energy practical and suggest two improvements, explaining the effect on the result.
exit: Which reagent tests for starch?
Why must the Benedict's tube be heated?
Why is energy measured by burning always an underestimate?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Describe how you would test a food sample for protein and for glucose.' (4 marks). Write a full answer with colour changes.
lessons.send: Support: table with reagent and colour pre-filled for matching. EAL: colour-coded vocabulary cards. Stretch: link to the energy value labels on food packaging.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: A balanced diet: nutrients, sources and energy needs
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do a teenager and an office worker of the same mass need different amounts of food?
objectives: To understand what a balanced diet contains and why energy needs vary
successCriteria: All: name the seven components of a balanced diet with a source each
Most: state the functions of vitamins A, C, D, calcium and iron
Some: explain differences in energy requirements
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology (food): planning balanced meals
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: eating in moderation as the Sunnah teaches

keywords.def: all nutrients in the right proportions
fats and oils: energy store and insulation
needed in small amounts for health
elements such as calcium and iron needed for health
indigestible plant material that helps food move through the gut

hook.text: If you could only eat one food for a month, which would keep you healthiest? Why can no single food do the job?
hook.a: No single food contains all nutrients in the right proportions.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught moderation: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink and a third for breath (at-Tirmidhi). Allah says: 'Eat and drink, but do not be wasteful' (al-A'raf 7:31).

starter.q: Which nutrient is the main source of energy?

teach.heading: The seven components
bullets: Proportion matters: more carbohydrate than lipid
teach.note: Ask pupils to name a food that is a good source of each. The word 'balanced' means the right amounts for that person, not equal amounts.

teach.heading: Vitamins and minerals you must know
bullets: Vitamin C: skin, gums and blood vessels
teach.note: Link each to its deficiency: A (night blindness), C (scurvy), D (rickets), calcium (weak bones and teeth), iron (anaemia). Vitamin D can be made in skin in sunlight, so it is also in oily fish, eggs and fortified foods.

teach.heading: Check: link nutrient to job
teach.note: Most will choose iron correctly; the vitamin D option is the common trap.

check.q: A girl is tired and pale and has a low red blood cell count. Which nutrient is she most likely to be short of?
check.why: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, so a shortage causes anaemia. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, vitamin D deficiency rickets, and low fibre causes constipation.

teach.heading: Energy requirements vary
bullets: Pregnancy needs extra energy and nutrients
Older adults are less active, so need less
teach.note: Give the idea, not memorised numbers. A very active person such as a builder or athlete needs more energy than someone at a desk. Adults over about 60 usually need less energy as metabolic rate and activity fall (approx.). A pregnant woman needs extra energy, protein, iron and calcium for the baby.

teach.heading: Model: explain a difference
bullets: Compare two people in a table
State the factor, then the reason
teach.note: Model the structure: factor, then because...

model.problem: A 15-year-old footballer needs more energy per day than a 70-year-old retired teacher. Explain why.
steps: The footballer is very active, so muscles respire faster and use more energy
He is still growing, so energy is needed to build new tissue
The older person is less active and no longer growing
model.answer: Higher activity level and growth give the footballer a greater energy requirement

teach.heading: Misconception: fibre and water
bullets: Fibre has no value because it is not digested
Water does not count as a nutrient
teach.note: Both are needed.

misconception.wrong: Fibre is useless because we cannot digest it
misconception.right: Fibre adds bulk so muscles can push food along by peristalsis and prevents constipation

practice.q: State the function of iron and a good source. [2 marks]
practice.a: Needed to make haemoglobin (1); red meat, spinach or lentils (1).
practice.model:
Function: iron is part of haemoglobin in red blood cells, which carries oxygen.
Source: red meat or lentils.
Two points, two marks.

practice.q: Which vitamin helps the body absorb calcium?
Why do we need fibre?
practice.a: It helps food move through the gut (prevents constipation).

independent.q: Core: Plan a balanced day's meals for a Year 10 pupil. Label each food with the nutrient it mainly provides.
independent.a: Accept balanced plans: e.g. porridge (carbohydrate, fibre), lentil soup (protein), fish (protein, vitamin D), fruit (vitamin C), water.
independent.model: Teacher labels breakfast first: porridge with milk: carbohydrate and fibre from oats, protein and calcium from milk.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why a pregnant woman needs more energy and iron. [2 marks]
independent.a: Extra energy for the growing fetus (1); extra iron for more blood for herself and the baby (1).

independent.q: Stretch: A 15-year-old needs more energy than a 70-year-old of the same mass. Explain. [2 marks]
independent.a: Teenagers are growing (1) and usually more active, so respire more (1).

exit.q: Which is needed for strong bones and teeth?
Big question: why do a teenager and an office worker need different amounts of food?
exit.a: Energy needs depend on age, growth and activity.

lessons.homework: Record everything you eat in one day and check it against the seven components.
lessons.send: SEND: nutrient picture cards. EAL: nutrient names with foods. Stretch: link deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, anaemia) to nutrients.

lessons.title: Digestive enzymes and bile
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does your body need both enzymes and bile to digest a fatty meal?
objectives: To understand how digestive enzymes and bile break down food into molecules small enough to absorb
successCriteria: All: name the enzymes that digest starch, protein and lipid and their products
Most: describe where bile is made, stored and what it does
Some: explain how emulsification and pH help lipase work
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: neutralisation and surface area in rates of reaction
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for the hidden work of digestion

keywords.def: enzyme that digests starch to maltose
enzyme that digests protein to amino acids
enzyme that digests lipids to fatty acids and glycerol
alkaline liquid from the liver that emulsifies fats
break fat into tiny droplets

hook.text: Washing-up liquid helps water clean a greasy pan. What in your body does a similar job?
hook.a: Bile emulsifies fat into tiny droplets, giving lipase more surface area.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Then let the human being look at his food' ('Abasa 80:24), and 'Eat and drink, but do not be wasteful' (al-A'raf 7:31). Digestion is one of the systems Allah made to turn food into the body's building blocks and energy.

starter.q: Name the seven components of a balanced diet.
starter.a: Carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water

teach.heading: Enzymes of the gut
bullets: Lipase: lipid to fatty acids and glycerol
teach.note: Remind pupils that enzymes are specific: one enzyme fits one substrate. Amylase is made in the salivary glands and pancreas; maltase is on the lining of the small intestine; proteases such as pepsin work in the stomach and others in the small intestine; lipase comes from the pancreas.

teach.heading: Bile: made, stored, released
teach.note: Trace bile on a diagram: liver, gall bladder, bile duct, duodenum. Many pupils think bile digests fat chemically; it does not, it only prepares the fat.

teach.heading: What bile does
bullets: Gives suitable pH for intestinal enzymes
teach.note: Link to enzyme work: the stomach acid is about pH 2 which would denature the intestinal enzymes. Emulsification is physical, not chemical.

left.title: Neutralising acid
points: Raises pH from the stomach's acid
Enzymes in intestine work best at alkaline pH

right.title: Emulsifying lipids
points: Large droplets split into small ones

teach.heading: Model: explain a data point
bullets: Link to surface area or pH
teach.note: Walk through the three-part answer.

model.problem: Explain why lipids are digested faster in the small intestine when bile is present.
steps: Bile emulsifies lipids, breaking large droplets into many small droplets
This increases the surface area of lipid available
Lipase can act on more lipid at once, so digestion is faster
model.answer: Emulsification increases the surface area for lipase to work on

teach.heading: Check: what does bile do?
teach.note: The common wrong choice is digesting fat chemically.

check.q: Which statement about bile is correct?
options: It is made in the gall bladder and digests lipids
It is made in the liver and emulsifies lipids
It is made in the pancreas and neutralises acid
It is an enzyme that breaks down fats
check.why: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and it emulsifies lipids and neutralises acid. It is not an enzyme and it is not made in the pancreas.

practice.q: State where bile is made and stored. [2 marks]
practice.a: Made in the liver (1); stored in the gall bladder (1).
practice.model:
Two places, two marks.
Made: liver.
Stored: gall bladder.
Released into the small intestine (duodenum) after a meal.

practice.q: Name the products of protein digestion.
Name the enzyme that digests maltose.

independent.q: Core: Complete the digestion table: enzyme, where made, substrate, products, for amylase, maltase, protease and lipase.
independent.a: Amylase (salivary glands, pancreas): starch to maltose; maltase (small intestine): maltose to glucose; protease (stomach, pancreas): protein to amino acids; lipase (pancreas): lipids to fatty acids and glycerol.
independent.model: Teacher fills amylase: made in salivary glands and pancreas; starch to maltose.

independent.q: Extend: Explain two ways bile helps digestion. [4 marks] Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Bile is alkaline (1) so it neutralises stomach acid, giving a suitable pH for intestinal enzymes (1); it emulsifies lipids into small droplets (1), increasing surface area for lipase (1).

independent.q: Stretch: A person has their gall bladder removed. Suggest why they are advised to eat less fat.
independent.a: Bile cannot be stored and released in large amounts at mealtimes, so fat is emulsified less well.

exit.q: Bile contains...
Big question: why does your body need both enzymes and bile for a fatty meal?
exit.a: Lipase digests lipids; bile emulsifies them and neutralises acid so lipase works faster.

lessons.homework: Make a flow diagram of a cheese sandwich's journey through the gut, naming each enzyme.
lessons.send: SEND: table partly completed. EAL: enzyme names with substrate pictures. Stretch: design an experiment to show bile speeds up lipid digestion (phenolphthalein and milk).

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Photosynthesis practicals and net gas exchange
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you prove that a leaf needs light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll to make food?
objectives: Describe practicals that show oxygen is evolved and starch is made
Explain the need for light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll
Explain how net gas exchange depends on light intensity (Higher/Paper 2 only)
successCriteria: All: describe the starch test on a leaf
Most: interpret results of leaf experiments with foil and variegated leaves
Some: predict net gas exchange at different light intensities (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solvents and flammability; Maths: interpreting graphs
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: signs in plants that sustain all life

keywords.def: leaving a plant in the dark so it uses up its starch
a leaf with green and white areas
the overall exchange of gases after photosynthesis and respiration
the light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration rates are equal

starter: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
Name the pigment that absorbs light.
State one limiting factor of photosynthesis.

teach.heading: Testing a leaf for starch
bullets: Warm it in ethanol in a water bath
Add iodine solution: blue-black means starch
teach.note: Explain each step: boiling kills the cells and softens the leaf; ethanol removes chlorophyll so the colour change is visible; ethanol is flammable, so no naked flame, use a hot water bath. Starch is the stored product of photosynthesis.

teach.heading: Showing each requirement
bullets: Light: cover part of a leaf with foil
Carbon dioxide: use soda lime in a sealed bell jar
Destarch the plant in the dark first
teach.note: Controls matter: a control plant with carbon dioxide and a fully exposed leaf. Results: starch only in uncovered green parts with carbon dioxide.

teach.heading: Model: interpret a variegated leaf
teach.note: Ask pupils to sketch the expected result before showing it.

model.problem: A destarched variegated leaf is placed in light for a day and then tested with iodine. Only the green parts turn blue-black. What does this show?
steps: Blue-black means starch is present in the green parts
The white parts have no chlorophyll and no starch
So chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis

teach.heading: Oxygen evolution (pondweed)
bullets: Count bubbles or collect gas volume
Change light distance and record rate
Use a heat shield or water bath for temperature
teach.note: Test the gas with a glowing splint if collected. The distance from lamp is a way to change light intensity. Practical issues: bubble size varies, so measure volume if possible.

teach.heading: Net gas exchange (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Plants respire all the time, day and night
In the dark only respiration: CO2 out, O2 in
In bright light photosynthesis exceeds respiration
Net: CO2 taken in, O2 released
teach.note: Mark as Higher/Paper 2 only. Hydrogen-carbonate indicator: red at normal CO2, yellow when CO2 increases, purple when it decreases. At the compensation point there is no net change.

teach.heading: Check: net gas exchange (Higher/Paper 2 only)
teach.note: The trap is the idea that plants only respire at night.

check.q: A leaf in a tube with hydrogen-carbonate indicator turns yellow. What explains this?
options: The leaf is absorbing carbon dioxide
check.why: Yellow means carbon dioxide has increased, so the leaf is releasing more carbon dioxide by respiration than it takes in by photosynthesis, as in the dark.

practice: State why the leaf is boiled in ethanol.
What would you expect under a foil strip? Explain.
Define net gas exchange.
independent: Core: Write a method to show that light is needed for photosynthesis including destarching.
Extend: Explain the results from a leaf where the CO2 was removed.
Stretch (Higher/Paper 2 only): Sketch how net CO2 exchange changes from darkness to bright light and mark the compensation point.
exit: Which colour shows starch with iodine?
Why is the plant destarched?
What does yellow indicator show?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Describe an experiment to show that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.' (5 marks).
lessons.send: Support: step cards to sequence the starch test. EAL: bilingual keywords. Stretch: explain why the compensation point rises with higher temperature.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Transpiration and the environment (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a washing line dry faster on a windy day, and what has that got to do with a tree?
objectives: Describe the effect of humidity, wind speed, temperature and light intensity on transpiration rate
Explain each effect using evaporation and diffusion
Interpret potometer data
successCriteria: All: name the four factors and say whether each increases or decreases the rate
Most: explain each using the concentration gradient
Some: calculate transpiration rate from potometer measurements
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: volume of a cylinder; Geography: weather and climate
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: observing the water cycle in a single tree

keywords.def: loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata
the amount of water vapour in the air
apparatus that measures water uptake by a shoot
pores in the leaf surface that open and close

starter: Define transpiration.
Which tissue carries water up the plant?
What do guard cells control?

teach.heading: Four factors (Higher/Paper 2 only)
teach.note: State that these are Higher/Paper 2 only. Light opens the stomata; warm air increases evaporation and gives molecules more energy; wind removes water vapour from near the leaf; high humidity reduces the concentration gradient.

teach.heading: The concentration gradient idea
bullets: Inside the leaf the air is humid
Vapour diffuses out through open stomata
teach.note: Draw a leaf section and show the gradient. Stress that a smaller gradient means slower diffusion.

teach.heading: Model: use a potometer
bullets: Use volume of a cylinder: pi x r2 x length
teach.note: Choose a capillary radius of 0.5 mm. It is an estimate of transpiration because the shoot uses a little water.

model.problem: In a potometer the bubble moves 36 mm in 6 minutes. The capillary radius is 0.5 mm. Find the rate of water uptake in mm3 per minute.
steps: Volume = pi x 0.5 x 0.5 x 36 = about 28.3 mm3

teach.heading: Check: predict the effect
teach.note: Discuss why high humidity is the odd one out.

check.q: Which condition gives the fastest transpiration rate?
check.why: Warm, windy, dry and bright conditions each increase transpiration: faster evaporation, humid air removed, steeper gradient and open stomata.

teach.heading: Misconception: wind and temperature
bullets: Transpiration only happens in hot weather
teach.note: Plants transpire day and night but fastest in warm, dry, windy, bright conditions.

misconception.wrong: Wind cools the leaf so transpiration slows down
misconception.right: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the gradient steep, so transpiration speeds up

practice: State two factors that increase transpiration.
Why does high humidity reduce the rate?
What is the function of guard cells?
independent: Core: Complete a table of the four factors, direction of change and reason.
Extend: Predict and explain the result of a hair dryer on a shoot in a potometer.
Stretch: Calculate transpiration rate from a bubble that moves 24 mm in 4 minutes in a 1.0 mm radius capillary.
exit: How does wind increase transpiration?
Why does light matter?
What does a potometer measure?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Explain why the rate of transpiration is higher on a warm, windy day than on a cool, calm day.' (4 marks).
lessons.send: Support: diagram with arrows to label the gradient. EAL: key words matched to pictures. Stretch: wilting and why a plant may close stomata on a hot day.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Blood: plasma, red cells and platelets
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a red blood cell shaped like a doughnut with a dent instead of a hole?
objectives: State what plasma transports
Explain how red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen
Describe how platelets cause blood clotting (Higher/Paper 2 only)
successCriteria: All: list the substances carried in plasma
Most: explain three red blood cell adaptations
Some: describe the clotting process and why it matters (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: reversible reactions; PSHE: first aid for bleeding
lessons.smsc: Moral: donating blood and helping others (sadaqah) as a medical act of care

keywords.def: the pale yellow liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances
red protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen
curved inwards on both sides, like a disc with a dip
small cell fragments that help blood to clot

starter: Name the four components of blood.
What does a phagocyte do?
State the function of the nucleus.

teach.heading: What plasma carries
bullets: Carbon dioxide from tissues to lungs
Digested food such as glucose and amino acids
Urea from the liver to the kidneys
Hormones and heat around the body
teach.note: Plasma is about 90 per cent water (approx.), with dissolved substances. Heat is spread from active organs such as muscles and liver to the rest of the body. Do not confuse plasma with serum or with blood as a whole.

teach.heading: Red blood cells: built for oxygen
bullets: Biconcave disc: large surface area to volume ratio
No nucleus: more room for haemoglobin
Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs
teach.note: Link back to SA:V and diffusion. Haemoglobin plus oxygen makes oxyhaemoglobin in the lungs where oxygen is plentiful; it releases oxygen where oxygen is low. The flexible shape helps them squeeze through capillaries.

teach.heading: Model: explain an adaptation
teach.note: Model the three-part structure.

model.problem: Explain how the absence of a nucleus helps a red blood cell carry oxygen.
steps: Red blood cells have no nucleus
This leaves more space inside the cell
More haemoglobin can be packed in, so more oxygen is carried
model.answer: No nucleus means more room for haemoglobin, so more oxygen is transported

teach.heading: Platelets and clotting (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: At a wound they help form a clot
A fibrin mesh traps blood cells to form a scab
Stops blood loss and blocks microbes
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. Fibrinogen (soluble) becomes fibrin (insoluble threads) when platelets and clotting factors are activated. The scab protects until new skin grows. Haemophilia is an inherited failure of clotting (extension).

teach.heading: Check: plasma and red cells
teach.note: The trap is oxygen being carried in plasma.

check.q: Which substance is carried mainly by red blood cells rather than plasma?
check.why: Most oxygen is bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells. Urea, glucose and hormones are dissolved in plasma.

practice: Name three things carried by plasma.
Why are red blood cells biconcave?
Higher: What are platelets?
independent: Core: Draw and annotate a red blood cell with three adaptations.
Extend: Explain why a person living at high altitude may make more red blood cells.
Stretch (Higher/Paper 2 only): Explain why clotting is important and what might happen if platelets are missing.
exit: State the function of haemoglobin.
What does plasma carry from the liver to the kidneys?
Higher: Name the protein mesh of a clot.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph linking the structure and function of a red blood cell and plasma.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagram to complete. EAL: bilingual word cards. Stretch: relate carbon monoxide poisoning to haemoglobin.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Heart rate, exercise and adrenaline
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does your heart pound when you run, and again when you are frightened?
objectives: Explain why heart rate rises during exercise
Describe the effect of adrenaline on the heart
Interpret heart rate data and recovery time
successCriteria: All: state that heart rate increases during exercise and with adrenaline
Most: explain why using oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide
Some: analyse recovery data and calculate percentage change
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentage change and graphs; PE: fitness and recovery
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awareness of the body as an amanah (trust)

keywords.def: hormone from the adrenal glands that prepares the body for action
the number of heartbeats per minute
time for heart rate to return to resting level after exercise
the pressure wave in an artery caused by each heartbeat

starter: Name the four chambers of the heart.
Which gas is a waste product of respiration?
What is a hormone?

teach.heading: Heart rate in exercise
bullets: They need more oxygen and glucose
Carbon dioxide level in blood rises
Brain raises heart rate, so blood flows faster
teach.note: The brain detects the higher carbon dioxide level and signals the heart to beat faster. Faster blood flow supplies oxygen and glucose and removes carbon dioxide and heat.

teach.heading: Adrenaline
bullets: Acts on the heart: beats faster and harder
teach.note: Adrenaline travels in the blood plasma; it is a hormone so it acts more slowly than nerves but lasts longer. It also widens the pupils and raises blood glucose; blood is diverted to muscles. Connect to existing hormone lessons.

teach.heading: Model: percentage increase
teach.note: Show the calculation line by line.

model.problem: A student's heart rate rises from 70 beats per minute at rest to 150 beats per minute after running. Find the percentage increase.
steps: x 100 = 114 per cent (to nearest whole number)

teach.heading: Reading recovery data
bullets: Recovery time = minutes to return to resting rate
teach.note: Present a table of two students; pupils compare recovery and suggest why. Keep to data, not claims about fitness levels.

teach.heading: Check: why does it rise?
teach.note: The distractors mix up cause and effect.

check.q: What is the main reason heart rate increases during exercise?
options: To deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove carbon dioxide
To increase the volume of blood
check.why: Active muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration and produce more carbon dioxide, so blood must flow faster.

practice: Name the gland that makes adrenaline.
Calculate the percentage increase from 60 to 135 beats per minute.
Why does faster blood flow help muscles?
independent: Core: Plot a graph of heart rate before, during and after exercise from given data and describe it.
Extend: Explain why a fitter person has a shorter recovery time.
Stretch: Explain why adrenaline has an effect on the heart in addition to the nervous system.
exit: State two effects of adrenaline.
Why does heart rate rise in exercise?
What is recovery time?
lessons.homework: Measure your pulse at rest and after one minute of star jumps (if safe), record and calculate the percentage change.
lessons.send: Support: calculation frame. EAL: sentence starters. Stretch: heart rate and stroke volume (extension, outside the spec).
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The urinary system and the nephron (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a pair of organs the size of your fist clean all of your blood?
objectives: Name and locate the parts of the urinary system
Describe the structure of a nephron
Link each part of the nephron to its function
successCriteria: All: name kidney, ureter, bladder and urethra and their jobs
Most: label the nephron
Some: explain how structure suits function
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solutions; PSHE: health and hydration
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the body, as a trust

keywords.def: tube carrying urine from kidney to bladder
tube carrying urine out of the body from the bladder
microscopic filtering unit of the kidney
knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule

starter: Name two excretory organs.
What is urea and where is it made?
Define excretion.

teach.heading: The urinary system (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Ureters carry urine to the bladder
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. Renal artery brings blood to the kidney and the renal vein takes cleaned blood away. Ask pupils to trace a drop of urine through the system.

teach.heading: Inside the kidney: the nephron
bullets: Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
teach.note: Each kidney has about a million nephrons (approx.). Sketch the nephron in order and let pupils copy.

head: Part
What it is
Role
rows: Carries urine to ureter; water reabsorbed

teach.heading: Model: trace the filtrate
bullets: Name the part, then say what happens
teach.note: Tell the story in order from the capsule outwards.

model.problem: Describe the path taken by a molecule of urea from the blood to the urethra.
steps: Filtered out of the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule
Flows along the tubule, loop of Henle and collecting duct
Leaves the kidney in the ureter, is stored in the bladder and passes out through the urethra
model.answer: Glomerulus, capsule, tubule, collecting duct, ureter, bladder, urethra

teach.heading: Check: identify the part
teach.note: Common error: confusing ureter and urethra.

check.q: Which part of the nephron is the knot of capillaries where blood is filtered?
check.why: The glomerulus is the capillary knot. The Bowman's capsule is the cup around it, and the loop of Henle and collecting duct are tubules.

teach.heading: Misconception: ureter and urethra
teach.note: Use memory trick: ureter = from kidney; urethra = out of the body.

misconception.wrong: The ureter carries urine out of the body
misconception.right: The ureters carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder; the urethra carries it out

practice: Name the organ that stores urine.
Where is the glomerulus found?
Why are there many nephrons in each kidney?
independent: Core: Label a nephron diagram and a urinary system diagram.
Extend: Explain how the structure of the glomerulus suits filtration.
Stretch: Compare the renal artery with the renal vein in terms of urea concentration.
exit: Name the tube that carries urine out of the body.
What is the Bowman's capsule?
Which part collects urine from many nephrons?
lessons.homework: Draw a flow chart showing the path of blood and urine through the kidney.
lessons.send: Support: pre-drawn outline with word bank. EAL: bilingual labels. Stretch: describe how the kidney can be replaced by dialysis.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Ultrafiltration and reabsorption of glucose (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would a drop of sugar in your urine tell a doctor something is wrong?
objectives: Explain ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule
State the composition of glomerular filtrate
Explain selective reabsorption of glucose in the proximal convoluted tubule
successCriteria: All: state which substances are filtered and which are not
Most: explain why high pressure is needed
Some: explain why glucose appears in urine if blood glucose is very high
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solutions and particle size; Maths: percentages
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: balance and precision in the body

keywords.def: filtration under high pressure forcing small molecules out of the blood
fluid in the Bowman's capsule containing small molecules from the blood
taking back useful substances into the blood from the filtrate
first coiled tubule after the Bowman's capsule

starter: What is the function of the glomerulus?
Describe active transport.
Name two substances found in urine.

teach.heading: Ultrafiltration (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Blood enters the glomerulus at high pressure
The efferent vessel is narrower than the afferent
Small molecules are forced into the capsule
Large molecules and cells stay in the blood
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. Pressure builds because the vessel leaving the glomerulus is narrower than the one entering. Filtration is not selective by usefulness; it is by size.

teach.heading: Selective reabsorption
bullets: Happens in the proximal convoluted tubule
Cells have many mitochondria and microvilli
teach.note: Link to active transport against the concentration gradient. Also amino acids, many ions and much water return to the blood; urea mostly stays. Microvilli increase surface area.

teach.heading: Model: explain glucose in urine
bullets: Use the idea of a limit on reabsorption
teach.note: Make explicit that carrier proteins can be saturated.

model.problem: A person with untreated diabetes has glucose in their urine. Explain why.
steps: Blood glucose is very high so a lot of glucose is filtered into the capsule
The carriers in the proximal tubule can only transport a limited amount
Extra glucose is not reabsorbed and passes out in urine
model.answer: The reabsorption mechanism is overwhelmed, so glucose stays in the urine

teach.heading: Model: how much is reabsorbed?
bullets: Typical figures (approx.): about 180 dm3 filtered per day
About 1.5 dm3 of urine passes out
teach.note: These are textbook approximations. The point is that almost all of the filtrate returns to the blood. Verify the figures against your textbook before quoting.

model.problem: About 180 dm3 of filtrate forms per day and about 1.5 dm3 of urine is produced (approx.). Estimate the percentage reabsorbed.
model.answer: About 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed (approx.)

teach.heading: Check: glomerular filtrate
teach.note: Most common error: thinking blood proteins are filtered.

check.q: Which substance is NOT normally found in the glomerular filtrate?
check.why: Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the glomerulus. Glucose, urea and water are small enough to be filtered.

practice: Why is the blood pressure high in the glomerulus?
Where is glucose reabsorbed?
Name two substances in urine.
independent: Core: Complete a table of filtered, reabsorbed and excreted substances.
Extend: Explain why the proximal tubule cells contain many mitochondria.
Stretch: Compare the glucose concentration in the filtrate, the end of the proximal tubule and urine.
exit: What is ultrafiltration?
Which process reabsorbs glucose?
Why does glucose appear in urine in diabetes?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Explain how the structure of the nephron allows it to filter blood and reabsorb glucose.' (6 marks).
lessons.send: Support: sorting cards for 'filtered' or 'stays in blood'. EAL: key terms in table. Stretch: link to kidney function tests (verify content).
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The nervous system: CNS, impulses and synapses
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a signal cross a gap that is far narrower than a hair?
objectives: Describe the central nervous system and how it links to sense organs
Explain how receptors send electrical impulses along nerves
Describe how neurotransmitters transmit signals across synapses
successCriteria: All: name the parts of the CNS and give the role of nerves
Most: describe the order from stimulus to response
Some: explain why synapses make transmission one-way
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: electrical signals; PE: reaction times
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at rapid, coordinated responses

keywords.def: the brain and spinal cord
a cell or organ that detects a stimulus
a nerve cell that carries electrical impulses
a gap between two neurones
chemical that diffuses across a synapse to pass on a signal

starter: Name the neurone that carries an impulse to a muscle.
What is a stimulus?
What are effectors?

teach.heading: Structure of the nervous system
bullets: Nerves link sense organs to the CNS
Nerves link the CNS to muscles and glands
teach.note: Show the stimulus, receptor, coordinator, effector, response chain. Sense organs include eye, ear, skin, nose and tongue.

teach.heading: Electrical impulses
teach.note: Compare with hormones, which travel in the blood. Impulses are electrical signals, not 'electricity' in the mains sense.

teach.heading: Synapses
bullets: Impulse reaches the end of neurone 1
Neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across
It binds receptors on neurone 2 and starts a new impulse
teach.note: Because only the first neurone releases neurotransmitter, the impulse goes one way. The delay is tiny.

teach.heading: Model: explain one-way transmission
bullets: Say who releases and who has receptors
teach.note: Spell out the logic carefully.

model.problem: Explain why an impulse travels in one direction across a synapse.
steps: Only the first neurone releases neurotransmitter into the gap
Only the second neurone has receptors for it
So the signal can only pass from the first to the second
model.answer: Neurotransmitter is released on one side only and the receptors are on the other side

teach.heading: Check: crossing the gap
teach.note: The trap is believing the electrical impulse jumps the gap.

check.q: How does a signal cross a synapse?
options: A hormone is released into the blood
check.why: A chemical, the neurotransmitter, diffuses across the gap and triggers a new impulse; the impulse itself does not cross.

practice: What is the CNS?
Give the role of a receptor.
Name the chemical that crosses a synapse.
independent: Core: Complete a flow diagram from stimulus to response for touching a hot pan.
Extend: Compare nervous and hormonal communication in a table.
Stretch: Explain why drugs that block neurotransmitter receptors can affect the nervous system.
exit: What carries information from the receptor?
What happens at a synapse?
State one difference between nerves and hormones.
lessons.homework: Make a labelled diagram of a synapse and write three sentences to explain it.
lessons.send: Support: sequencing cards for the synapse. EAL: bilingual vocabulary. Stretch: link to reaction time practical.
