lessons.unit: Spring 2: Transport, the periodic table and waves
lessons.title: Why multicellular organisms need transport systems
lessons.bigQuestion: An amoeba needs no heart or lungs, yet an elephant cannot live without them. What changes as organisms get bigger?
objectives: To understand why large organisms need transport systems while single cells can rely on diffusion
successCriteria: All: calculate surface area to volume ratio for cubes
Most: explain why ratio falls as size increases
Some: link SA:V to the need for lungs, gut and circulation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: surface area, volume and ratio
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: design in the size and shape of living things

keywords.def: surface area divided by volume; falls as an organism gets bigger
net movement of particles from high to low concentration
made of one cell
made of many cells
a system that carries substances around the body

hook.text: An amoeba needs no heart or lungs, yet an elephant cannot live without them. What changes as organisms get bigger?
hook.a: Surface area to volume ratio falls, so diffusion alone cannot supply the inner cells fast enough.

starter.q: Name the process that moves oxygen into the blood in the alveoli.
Which blood vessel has the thickest muscular wall?
State one factor that increases the rate of diffusion.
starter.a: Larger surface area, steeper gradient, shorter distance or higher temperature

teach.heading: Unicellular organisms
teach.note: Spec 2.51. Amoeba, bacteria.

teach.heading: SA:V of cubes
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Find the SA:V ratio of a 1 cm cube and a 4 cm cube.
steps: 1 cm cube: SA = 6 × 1² = 6 cm²; V = 1 cm³; ratio 6:1
4 cm cube: SA = 6 × 4² = 96 cm²; V = 4³ = 64 cm³
model.answer: 6:1 and 1.5:1: the bigger cube has a much smaller ratio

teach.heading: Why big organisms need systems
bullets: Inner cells far from the surface
Diffusion too slow over long distances
teach.note: Spec 2.52. Lungs, gut villi and circulation in humans; xylem and phloem in plants.

items: Exchange surfaces: alveoli, villi, root hairs, leaves

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which has the largest SA:V?
check.why: Smaller objects have larger SA:V: 6, 3 and 2 per cm for 1, 2 and 3 cm cubes.

practice.q: Calculate SA:V for a 2 cm cube. [2 marks]
Explain why a flatworm does not need a circulatory system. [2 marks]
practice.a: It is very thin/flat so has a large SA:V (1); all cells are close to the surface, so diffusion is fast enough (1)

practice.q: Give two exchange surfaces in humans.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 4 marks): Explain why mammals need both a gas exchange surface and a circulatory system. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Large multicellular so small SA:V (1); diffusion distance to inner cells too long (1); lungs give large surface for gas exchange (1); blood carries oxygen and glucose to all cells and removes CO₂ (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'Mammals are large, so they have a small surface area to volume ratio.'

independent.q: Extend: Agar cube practical data: 1 cm cube coloured through in 4 min, 2 cm cube in 15 min. Explain. [2 marks]
independent.a: Larger cube has smaller SA:V (1) and longer distance to centre, so diffusion takes longer (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why do elephants have large thin ears in hot climates?
independent.a: Large SA for losing heat by radiation; thin with many blood vessels near the surface.

exit.q: As size increases, SA:V...
Big question: why does an elephant need a heart and lungs but an amoeba does not?
exit.a: Its SA:V is small, so diffusion alone cannot supply inner cells; exchange surfaces and transport are needed.

lessons.homework: Complete the SA:V question set on the portal (8 questions, 20 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: cube net to count faces. EAL: surface area, volume, ratio. Stretch: calculate SA:V for a 1 × 1 × 10 cm cuboid and comment on shape.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Transport, the periodic table and waves
lessons.title: Transport in plants: xylem and phloem
lessons.bigQuestion: A tree can lift water over 100 m without a pump. What sort of tubes would you need to do that?
objectives: To understand how xylem and phloem transport substances through a flowering plant
successCriteria: All: state what xylem and phloem carry
Most: describe the structure of xylem and phloem
Some: explain why the celery dye practical shows xylem
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: water in the water cycle through plants
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: water raised in trees without any pump

keywords.def: dead, hollow, lignified tubes carrying water and mineral ions up from roots
living tubes carrying sucrose and amino acids around the plant
movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem
strong substance in xylem walls
a group of xylem and phloem vessels

hook.text: A tree can lift water over 100 m without a pump. What sort of tubes would you need to do that?
hook.a: Long, hollow, strong-walled tubes with no cross walls (xylem), with water pulled up as it evaporates from leaves.

starter.q: Which mineral ion is needed to make chlorophyll?
Why do large organisms need transport?

teach.heading: Two transport tissues
bullets: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards
Phloem: sucrose and amino acids, up and down
teach.note: Spec 2.53 and 2.54.

teach.heading: Where they are
teach.note: Show cross-section micrographs: xylem inner, phloem outer in a stem bundle.

teach.heading: Phloem: source to sink
bullets: Sucrose carried to roots, fruits, growing tips (sinks)
teach.note: Sucrose, not glucose, is transported.

teach.heading: Dye practical
teach.note: Home practical safety: adult cuts with a knife; food colouring stains.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which tissue carries sucrose?
check.why: Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids; xylem carries water and ions.

practice.q: Give two ways xylem is adapted to transport water. [2 marks]
practice.a: Hollow with no end walls so water flows freely (1); lignin strengthens walls so they do not collapse (1)
practice.model: Think structure then function. No end walls: continuous tube. Lignin: strong walls. Each linked to how water moves.

practice.q: Name the substances carried in phloem. [2 marks]
Why is phloem called two-way?
practice.a: It carries substances up and down, from sources to sinks

independent.q: Core: Celery practical at home with an adult (celery in coloured water for 24 h, cut across, magnifier). Draw the cross-section and label xylem; answer: 'Explain your observations.' [3 marks]
independent.a: Coloured dots in a ring (1); these are xylem vessels (1); water and dye moved up the xylem from the base (1)
independent.model: Teacher shows a cut celery stem on camera and labels the first coloured dot 'xylem vessel'.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Compare transport in xylem and phloem.
independent.a: Xylem carries water and ions; phloem carries sucrose and amino acids (1); xylem one direction, phloem both (1); xylem dead hollow cells, phloem living (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Aphids feed on plant sap from the stem. Which tissue do they pierce, and how could you tell?
independent.a: Phloem: their honeydew is sugary.

exit.q: Water moves up through the...
Big question: what tubes lift water up a tree?
exit.a: Xylem: long, hollow, lignified tubes with no end walls.

lessons.send: SEND: xylem and phloem comparison table to complete. EAL: xylem (up), phloem (food). Stretch: research transpiration (Biology-only) and how leaves pull water.

lessons.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
lessons.bigQuestion: Potassium is kept under oil, yet sodium chloride is safe enough to eat. How can the same family be so dangerous and so harmless?
objectives: To understand how the reactions of Group 1 metals show they are a family with a reactivity trend
successCriteria: All: describe the reactions of Li, Na and K with water
Most: write balanced symbol equations for them
Some: use the trend to predict the properties of rubidium and caesium
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: interpreting trends in data

keywords.def: an element in Group 1
a compound containing OH⁻; Group 1 hydroxides are alkalis
go dull as a surface oxide forms
how readily an element reacts
a gradual change down a group

hook.text: Potassium is kept under oil, yet sodium chloride is safe enough to eat. How can the same family be so dangerous and so harmless?
hook.a: The metals are very reactive; their compounds are stable because the reaction has already happened.

starter.q: Group 1 elements have ... electron(s) in their outer shell.
What is the test for hydrogen?
starter.a: Lit splint gives a squeaky pop
options: Lit splint gives a squeaky pop

teach.heading: Similar reactions (spec 2.1)
bullets: All react with water: metal hydroxide + hydrogen
teach.note: Teacher demonstration on camera in the school laboratory, or a recorded demonstration with no music behind a safety screen: Li, Na, K in water with universal indicator.

teach.heading: Observations (spec 2.2)
teach.note: Pupils record during the demonstration.

head: Metal
With water
In air (cut surface)
rows: floats, melts into a ball, moves, fizzes

teach.heading: Balanced equation
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Write the balanced symbol equation for sodium with water, with state symbols.
steps: Word: sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen

teach.heading: Predicting (spec 2.3)
bullets: Rubidium and caesium: even more reactive
Lower melting points down the group
teach.note: Electronic explanation (2.4C) is Chemistry-only: not examined in 4SD0.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Universal indicator after potassium reacts with water turns...
check.why: Potassium hydroxide is a strong alkali, pH about 14.

practice.q: Write the balanced equation for lithium with water. [2 marks]
practice.model: Same pattern as sodium: metal + water → hydroxide + hydrogen. Li + H₂O → LiOH + H₂. Hydrogens: 2 on the left need H₂ on the right, so double: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂.

practice.q: Describe two observations when sodium is added to water. [2 marks]
practice.a: Any two: floats; melts into a ball; moves around; fizzes; gets smaller and disappears

practice.q: Predict how caesium reacts with water.
practice.a: Explosively, forming caesium hydroxide and hydrogen

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 5 marks): Rubidium is below potassium. Predict and explain its reaction with water, including a balanced equation. Portal response box.
independent.a: Reacts more vigorously than potassium/explosively (1); because reactivity increases down Group 1 (1); forms rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen (1); 2Rb + 2H₂O → 2RbOH + H₂ (2)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'Rubidium would react more violently than potassium, because reactivity increases down Group 1.'

independent.q: Extend (2 marks): Why are Group 1 metals stored under oil?
independent.a: They react with oxygen and water vapour in air (1); oil keeps air and water away (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Melting points: Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C. Estimate Rb's and justify.
independent.a: About 40 °C (actual 39 °C): the trend decreases by smaller steps.

exit.q: Group 1 + water → hydroxide + ...
Big question: why is sodium chloride safe but sodium dangerous?
exit.a: Sodium is very reactive; in sodium chloride it has already reacted to form a stable compound.

lessons.bigQuestion: A Mexican wave travels round a stadium, but nobody leaves their seat. What has actually moved round the stadium?
objectives: To understand how waves transfer energy and how to describe them with amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed
successCriteria: All: label amplitude and wavelength on a wave diagram
Most: distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves
Some: use v = fλ and f = 1/T

keywords.def: maximum displacement from the rest position
distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next
number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz)
time for one complete wave
vibrations at right angles to the direction of energy transfer

hook.text: A Mexican wave travels round a stadium, but nobody leaves their seat. What has actually moved round the stadium?
hook.a: Energy (and the pattern), not the people: waves transfer energy, not matter.

starter.q: Which wave can travel through a vacuum: light or sound?

teach.heading: Waves transfer energy (spec 3.4)
bullets: The medium does not travel with the wave
Particles oscillate about a fixed point
teach.note: Duck bobbing on a pond stays in place.

teach.heading: Transverse and longitudinal (spec 3.2)
teach.note: Slinky demonstration on camera.

teach.heading: Describing a wave (spec 3.3)
bullets: Frequency f in Hz; period T in s
Wavefront: line joining points in step
teach.note: Draw and label a transverse wave.

teach.heading: v = fλ (spec 3.5, 3.6)
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 0.4 m. Find its speed and period.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: A wave has a period of 0.5 s. Its frequency is...

practice.q: Sound of frequency 256 Hz has wavelength 1.3 m. Speed? [2 marks]
practice.model: Write v = fλ. Substitute 256 and 1.3. 256 × 1.3 = 332.8, so about 333 m/s.

practice.q: Is sound transverse or longitudinal?
A wave's period is 0.004 s. Frequency? [2 marks]

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): (a) Draw a transverse wave and label amplitude and wavelength [2]. (b) A water wave has speed 1.5 m/s and frequency 0.5 Hz. Find its wavelength [2]. (c) State what is transferred by the wave [1] and one difference from a longitudinal wave [1].
independent.a: (a) correct labels (2); (b) λ = v ÷ f = 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3 m (2); (c) energy (1); vibrations perpendicular rather than parallel to energy transfer (1)
independent.model: Teacher draws the wave on screen and labels the amplitude from the rest line to a crest.

independent.q: Extend: Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Find the wavelength of a 100 MHz station. [3 marks]
Stretch: Why does a cork bobbing on water not move towards the shore with the wave?
independent.a: Water particles oscillate about a fixed position; only energy moves.

exit.q: v = fλ: 10 Hz, 2 m gives...
Big question: what moves round the stadium in a Mexican wave?
exit.a: Energy and the wave pattern, not the people.

lessons.homework: Complete the wave calculations sheet on the portal (10 questions).
lessons.send: SEND: v = fλ triangle and unit card. EAL: crest, trough, oscillate. Stretch: prefixes kHz, MHz, GHz conversions.

keywords.def: a number written as A × 10ⁿ
3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum
a reflected sound wave

hook.text: Lightning strikes and you count 6 seconds before the thunder. How far away was it?
hook.a: About 340 × 6 ≈ 2000 m (2 km): light arrives almost instantly, sound at about 340 m/s.

starter.q: Speed of light in a vacuum?

teach.heading: Rearranging (spec 3.7)
teach.note: Always convert prefixes first.

teach.heading: Prefixes
teach.note: Common exam traps.

teach.heading: EM wave
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz microwaves. Find the wavelength.

teach.heading: Echo
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: A ship's sonar pulse returns after 0.8 s. Sound in water travels at 1500 m/s. How deep is the sea?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: A sound of 680 Hz in air (340 m/s) has wavelength...

practice.q: A radio station broadcasts at 200 kHz with wavelength 1500 m. Show the speed is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. [2 marks]
practice.model: Convert 200 kHz to 200 000 Hz. Multiply by 1500: 300 000 000 = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

practice.q: Thunder heard 3 s after lightning; sound 340 m/s. Distance?
Wavelength of green light is 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. Frequency? [2 marks]

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 8 marks): five-question set on the portal: sound and EM wave calculations with prefixes and echoes.
independent.a: Mark scheme on the sheet; e.g. 512 Hz at 340 m/s gives λ = 0.66 m; echo after 1.2 s at 340 m/s gives 204 m

independent.q: Extend: A clap echo from a wall 85 m away returns after 0.5 s. Calculate the speed of sound. [3 marks]
Stretch: Why do sound and light both obey v = fλ although one is longitudinal and one transverse?
independent.a: The equation follows from the definition of a wave (one wavelength passes per period) for any wave.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Transport, the periodic table and waves
lessons.title: Excretion in plants and animals
lessons.bigQuestion: Faeces leave the body, but biologists say this is NOT excretion. Why not?
objectives: To understand how plants and humans remove waste products of metabolism
successCriteria: All: define excretion and name the excretory products of lungs, kidneys and skin
Most: describe how oxygen and carbon dioxide leave plants through stomata
Some: explain the difference between excretion and egestion
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: drinking water and kidney health
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the body's cleansing systems

keywords.def: removal of waste products made by metabolism
nitrogen-containing waste made in the liver from excess amino acids
removal of undigested food (faeces)
pores in leaves for gas exchange
all the chemical reactions in an organism

hook.text: Faeces leave the body, but biologists say this is NOT excretion. Why not?
hook.a: Faeces are mostly undigested food that was never made by the body's cells: that is egestion.

starter.q: Which gas is a waste product of respiration?
Name the blood vessel that carries blood to the kidney.

teach.heading: Excretion vs egestion
teach.note: Spec 2.71.

teach.heading: Human excretory organs
teach.note: Spec 2.71. Kidney detail is Biology-only.

head: Organ
Excretes
rows: Urea, excess water and salts (in urine)
Water, salts and some urea (in sweat)

teach.heading: Plants (spec 2.70)
bullets: Daytime: oxygen from photosynthesis is a waste product
Both lost through stomata by diffusion
teach.note: Net exchange depends on light intensity.

teach.heading: Circulation links (spec 2.69)
bullets: Hepatic portal vein: gut to liver
teach.note: Liver makes urea; blood takes it to kidneys.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which is excretion?
check.why: CO₂ is a waste product of respiration, made by cells.

practice.q: Explain why carbon dioxide release from lungs is excretion. [2 marks]
practice.a: CO₂ is a waste product of respiration (1), a metabolic reaction in cells (1)
practice.model: Excretion means waste made by metabolism. Where does CO₂ come from? Respiration in cells. So it is excretion.

practice.q: Name the waste product made from excess amino acids and the organ that makes it. [2 marks]
Why do plants release oxygen in the day?
practice.a: Photosynthesis makes more oxygen than respiration uses

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 5 marks): Describe how the lungs, kidneys and skin excrete waste, and explain why faeces are not excretory products. Portal response box.
independent.a: Lungs: CO₂ (1); kidneys: urea, water, salts as urine (1); skin: sweat with water, salts, urea (1); faeces are undigested food (1), not made by metabolism, so egestion (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes 'The lungs excrete carbon dioxide, a waste product of respiration.'

independent.q: Extend: Trace urea from the liver to the bladder through named blood vessels and organs. [3 marks]
independent.a: Liver → hepatic vein → vena cava → heart → aorta → renal artery → kidney (1, 1); urine → ureter → bladder (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why does a plant in the dark release CO₂ but not O₂?
independent.a: No photosynthesis in the dark; respiration continues.

exit.q: Urea is made in the...
Big question: why are faeces not excreted?
exit.a: They are undigested food, not waste made by metabolism: egestion.

lessons.homework: Complete the excretion question set on the portal (timed, 15 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: organ and product matching cards. EAL: excrete, egest, urea. Stretch: research how dialysis replaces kidney function.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Transport, the periodic table and waves
lessons.title: Blood and the immune response
lessons.bigQuestion: You catch chickenpox once and almost never again. What has your blood 'remembered'?
objectives: To understand how blood cells transport oxygen and defend the body against pathogens
successCriteria: All: name the four components of blood and their roles
Most: explain the adaptations of red blood cells
Some: describe how phagocytes and lymphocytes defend the body
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: interpreting antibody response graphs
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the sick and preventing spread of disease

keywords.def: liquid part of blood carrying dissolved substances
protein in red cells that binds oxygen
white cell that engulfs and digests pathogens
white cell that produces antibodies
protein that binds to a specific antigen on a pathogen

hook.text: You catch chickenpox once and almost never again. What has your blood 'remembered'?
hook.a: Lymphocytes made specific antibodies; memory of that antigen means a faster response next time.

teach.heading: Blood components (spec 2.59, 2.60)
bullets: Plasma: CO₂, digested food, urea, hormones, heat
teach.note: Platelets and clotting detail is Biology-only.

teach.heading: Red blood cells (spec 2.61)
teach.note: Binds in lungs, releases in tissues.

teach.heading: The immune response (spec 2.62)
bullets: Antibodies fit antigens and clump pathogens
teach.note: Specific: one antibody type per antigen.

teach.heading: Why second infections are mild
teach.note: Vaccination is Biology-only; mention context only.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which cell produces antibodies?
check.why: Lymphocytes make antibodies; phagocytes engulf pathogens.

practice.q: Explain two adaptations of red blood cells. [4 marks]
practice.a: Biconcave shape (1) gives a large surface area for oxygen diffusion (1); no nucleus (1) leaves more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen (1)
practice.model: Feature then reason. Shape: biconcave, so large surface area. Nucleus: none, so more space for haemoglobin.

practice.q: Name three substances carried in plasma.
practice.a: Any three: CO₂, digested food (glucose, amino acids), urea, hormones (heat also transported)

practice.q: Why is an antibody specific? [1 mark]
practice.a: Its shape fits only one antigen

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how white blood cells protect the body when bacteria enter a cut. Portal response box.
independent.a: Phagocytes move to the bacteria (1), engulf them (1) and digest them with enzymes (1); lymphocytes recognise antigens (1), produce specific antibodies (1), which bind/clump bacteria so they are destroyed (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'Phagocytes are attracted to the bacteria and engulf them.'

independent.q: Extend: Explain why people living at high altitude develop more red blood cells. [2 marks]
independent.a: Less oxygen in the air (1); more red cells/haemoglobin carry enough oxygen to tissues (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses. Why must the immune system deal with viruses?
independent.a: Antibiotics target bacterial structures viruses lack; antibodies and lymphocytes still recognise viral antigens.

exit.q: Phagocytes...
Big question: what has your blood remembered after chickenpox?
exit.a: The antigen: memory lymphocytes make antibodies faster next time.

lessons.homework: Complete the blood and immunity question set on the portal (timed, 20 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: blood component cards. EAL: engulf, antibody, antigen. Stretch: research how monoclonal antibodies are used in pregnancy tests.

lessons.title: Group 7: the halogens and displacement
lessons.bigQuestion: Chlorine bubbled into a colourless potassium bromide solution turns it orange. What new substance has appeared, and why?
objectives: To understand the trends in Group 7 and how displacement reactions show their reactivity order
successCriteria: All: describe the colours and states of chlorine, bromine and iodine
Most: predict and write equations for halogen displacement
Some: use trends to predict properties of fluorine and astatine
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: interpreting data tables
lessons.smsc: Social: chlorine in safe drinking water

keywords.def: a Group 7 element
molecules made of two atoms, e.g. Cl₂
a compound or ion of a halogen, e.g. chloride Cl⁻
a more reactive halogen replaces a less reactive one in a compound
a gradual change down a group

hook.text: Chlorine bubbled into a colourless potassium bromide solution turns it orange. What new substance has appeared, and why?
hook.a: Bromine: chlorine is more reactive and displaces bromide ions.

teach.heading: Physical properties (spec 2.5)
teach.note: Colours and states at room temperature.

teach.heading: Trends (spec 2.6)
teach.note: Fluorine: pale yellow gas, most reactive; astatine: dark solid, least.

teach.heading: Displacement (spec 2.7)
bullets: More reactive halogen + halide of less reactive halogen
Colour change shows the new halogen
teach.note: Teacher demonstration on camera in the school laboratory, or a recorded demonstration with no music (halogen water added to halide solutions).

teach.heading: Writing the equation
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution. Write the balanced equation and describe the colour change.
steps: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces it
Colourless solution turns brown as iodine forms

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which mixture reacts?
check.why: Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodide.

practice.q: Write the balanced equation for bromine + sodium iodide. [2 marks]
practice.model: Bromine above iodine, so it displaces. Br₂ + NaI → NaBr + I₂; two iodides needed for I₂, so 2NaI and 2NaBr.

practice.q: Predict the state and colour of astatine at room temperature.
Why does iodine not react with potassium chloride?
practice.a: Iodine is less reactive than chlorine

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Complete the displacement results grid for Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ with KCl, KBr and KI (3), explain the pattern (1), and write one balanced equation (2).
independent.a: Cl₂ reacts with KBr and KI; Br₂ reacts with KI only; I₂ none (3); reactivity decreases down the group (1); e.g. Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (2)
independent.model: Teacher fills the chlorine row: 'No reaction with KCl; orange with KBr; brown with KI.'

independent.q: Extend (2 marks): Fluorine is above chlorine. Predict its reaction with sodium chloride solution in principle and its reactivity.
independent.a: Would displace chlorine (1) because it is the most reactive halogen (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why is hydrogen chloride gas not the same as chlorine gas in properties?
independent.a: It is a compound with different bonding and properties from the element Cl₂.

exit.q: Down Group 7 reactivity...
Big question: what made the solution orange?
exit.a: Bromine, displaced from potassium bromide by more reactive chlorine.

lessons.homework: Complete the Group 7 exam question set on the portal (timed, 20 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: reactivity ladder card. EAL: displace, halide. Stretch: write ionic equations, e.g. Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Transport, the periodic table and waves
lessons.title: The electromagnetic spectrum: uses and dangers
lessons.bigQuestion: Your phone, your toaster, the Sun and a hospital X-ray machine all use the same kind of wave. What is different about them?
objectives: To understand the order, uses and hazards of the electromagnetic spectrum
successCriteria: All: list the seven groups in order of wavelength and frequency
Most: give a use of each group
Some: explain the harmful effects of microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet and gamma and how to reduce them
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: satellite communications and remote sensing
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting patients and workers from radiation

keywords.def: the continuous family of transverse waves that travel at the speed of light in a vacuum
able to knock electrons out of atoms
radiation beyond violet light that can damage skin cells
highest-frequency electromagnetic waves
radiation we feel as heat

hook.text: Your phone, your toaster, the Sun and a hospital X-ray machine all use the same kind of wave. What is different about them?
hook.a: Wavelength and frequency: all are electromagnetic waves at different parts of the spectrum.

starter.q: Speed of light in a vacuum?
Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?

teach.heading: The spectrum (spec 3.10, 3.11)
bullets: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma
All travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum
teach.note: Visible: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

teach.heading: Uses (spec 3.12)
teach.note: Learn one use per group.

teach.heading: Dangers (spec 3.13)
bullets: Microwaves: internal heating of body tissue
Ultraviolet: damage to surface cells and eyes, skin cancer
teach.note: Protection: shielding, sunscreen and sunglasses, limiting exposure, lead aprons and distance.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which has the highest frequency?
check.why: Gamma rays are at the high-frequency, short-wavelength end.

practice.q: State one use and one danger of ultraviolet. [2 marks]
practice.a: Use: fluorescent lamps (or detecting forged banknotes) (1); danger: skin cancer or eye damage (1)
practice.model: Use from the spec list: fluorescent lamps. Danger: damages surface cells, so skin cancer and eye conditions.

practice.q: Put in order of increasing frequency: X-rays, microwaves, visible.
Why is gamma used to sterilise medical equipment?
practice.a: It kills microorganisms and passes through packaging

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): A hospital uses X-rays and gamma rays. (a) State one use of each [2]. (b) Explain why staff stand behind lead screens [2]. (c) Compare the frequency and speed of the two waves in a vacuum [2].
independent.a: (a) X-rays: images of bones; gamma: sterilising equipment or killing cancer cells (2); (b) ionising radiation can damage cells/cause mutations (1); lead absorbs it, reducing exposure (1); (c) gamma higher frequency (1); same speed (1)
independent.model: Teacher answers (a) aloud with the spec wording.

independent.q: Extend: Explain how infrared night-vision cameras work. [2 marks]
independent.a: Warm objects emit more infrared (1); the camera detects infrared and forms an image (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why microwaves can heat food but radio waves of the same power do not do so efficiently.
independent.a: Microwave frequencies are absorbed strongly by water molecules in food; radio waves mostly pass through.

exit.q: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a...
Big question: what is different about the phone, toaster and X-ray waves?
exit.a: Their wavelength and frequency; all are electromagnetic waves.

lessons.homework: Learn the spectrum in order with a mnemonic and one use and one danger for each group.
lessons.send: SEND: spectrum strip to colour. EAL: frequency, wavelength, ionising. Stretch: research why sunscreen labels show UVA and UVB.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Transport, the periodic table and waves
lessons.title: Coordination: the nervous system and reflexes
lessons.bigQuestion: You pull your hand off a hot pan before you even feel the pain. How is that possible?
objectives: To understand how the nervous system detects stimuli and coordinates fast responses, including reflexes
successCriteria: All: describe stimulus, receptor, coordinator, effector and response
Most: explain how impulses cross a synapse
Some: describe the reflex arc for withdrawing a hand from heat
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: road safety and reaction times
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the precision of the nervous system

keywords.def: a change in the environment
cells that detect a stimulus
a muscle or gland that produces a response
a gap between neurones crossed by neurotransmitter
a fast, automatic response that does not involve conscious thought

hook.text: You pull your hand off a hot pan before you even feel the pain. How is that possible?
hook.a: A reflex arc goes through the spinal cord, not the conscious brain, so the response is faster than the feeling.

starter.a: Eye, ear, nose, tongue or skin

starter.q: Bromine + potassium iodide: does it react?

teach.heading: Responding to change (spec 2.80, 2.82)
teach.note: Example: seeing a ball, catching it.

teach.heading: The nervous system (spec 2.87, 2.88)
bullets: Nerves link CNS to receptors and effectors
teach.note: Sensory, relay and motor neurones.

teach.heading: Synapses (spec 2.89)
bullets: Triggers impulse in the next neurone
teach.note: Ensures one-way transmission.

teach.heading: The reflex arc (spec 2.90)
bullets: Heat → receptor in skin → sensory neurone → relay neurone in spinal cord → motor neurone → muscle contracts
teach.note: Protects from harm; brain informed afterwards.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: In the hand-withdrawal reflex, the effector is...
check.why: Effectors carry out the response: the muscle contracts.

practice.q: Explain why a reflex is faster than a conscious response. [2 marks]
practice.a: The impulse passes through the spinal cord via a relay neurone (1), not through the conscious part of the brain, so fewer synapses and no decision time (1)
practice.model: Where does a conscious response go? To the brain to decide. A reflex goes through the spinal cord only. Shorter route, no thinking: faster.

practice.q: How does an impulse cross a synapse?
practice.a: A neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap

practice.q: Name the coordinator in the nervous system.
practice.a: The central nervous system (brain and spinal cord)

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe the pathway of the reflex arc when a finger touches a hot object. Portal response box.
independent.a: Heat is the stimulus (1); receptor in the skin (1); impulse along sensory neurone (1); relay neurone in spinal cord via synapses (1); motor neurone (1); effector muscle contracts, finger withdrawn (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first line: 'The stimulus is heat, detected by receptors in the skin.'

independent.q: Extend: Ruler-drop reaction test at home with an adult: catch a dropped ruler 5 times; record cm and calculate the mean. Is this a reflex? [2 marks]
independent.a: Mean distance recorded (1); not a reflex: it uses the brain and conscious decision (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Compare nervous and hormonal communication. [3 marks]
independent.a: Nervous: electrical impulses, fast, short-lived, precise; hormonal: chemicals in blood, slower, longer-lasting, widespread

exit.q: Neurotransmitters cross the...
Big question: how do you move your hand before feeling pain?
exit.a: A reflex arc through the spinal cord bypasses the conscious brain.

lessons.homework: Complete the nervous system question set on the portal (timed, 20 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: reflex arc cards to order. EAL: stimulus, receptor, effector. Stretch: research how some drugs affect synapses.

bullets: Light slows entering glass or water

practice.q: A ray enters water at 30° to the normal and refracts to 22°. Explain why it bent. [2 marks]
practice.a: Light slows down in water (1), so it changes direction towards the normal (1)
practice.model: What changed? The medium. What happens to speed? It slows. Slower, so it bends towards the normal: 30° became 22°.

practice.q: What angle of refraction occurs when i = 0°?
State the law of reflection.
practice.a: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Draw a ray entering and leaving a rectangular glass block at i = 40° (use the data: r = 25°) [4], and explain the emergent ray's direction [2].

independent.model: Teacher draws the block, the first normal and the incident ray on screen.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why a straw in a glass of water looks bent. [3 marks]
independent.a: Light from the straw refracts at the water surface (1), bending away from the normal into air (1); the brain traces rays back in straight lines, so the straw appears displaced (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why do waves refract when they slow down? Use wavefronts.
independent.a: One side of the wavefront enters the slower medium first and slows, so the wavefront turns.

exit.q: Angles are measured from the...

exit.a: No: refraction makes the bottom look higher than it is.

layer of light receptor cells

hook.text: How can the same eye read the small print on your hand and then focus on a far mountain a second later?
hook.a: Ciliary muscles change the lens shape: fatter for near objects, thinner for far ones.

islamicLink.text: Allah says He 'gave you hearing and sight and hearts, so that you may be grateful' (An-Nahl 16:78). The eye's ability to adjust in an instant is a sign worth reflecting on.

Far: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tight, lens thinner

check.q: Focusing on a near object, the lens becomes...

practice.q: Which part contains light receptors?

independent.model: Teacher writes: 'To focus on the near book, the ciliary muscles contract.'

independent.q: Extend: Why is the pupil reflex a reflex and not a conscious action? [2 marks]
independent.a: Automatic and fast (1); does not involve conscious thought; protects the retina (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Long-sightedness: the lens cannot become fat enough. Suggest which objects look blurred and why.
independent.a: Near objects: light is focused behind the retina.

exit.q: In dim light the pupil...
Big question: how does the eye focus near then far?
exit.a: Ciliary muscles change the lens: fatter for near, thinner for far.

hook.text: Internet data crosses oceans as flashes of light inside glass thinner than a hair. Why doesn't the light leak out of the sides?
hook.a: It hits the inside surface above the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected every time.

teach.heading: Critical angle (spec 3.21)
teach.note: Semicircular block demonstration on camera or simulation.

teach.heading: TIR conditions (spec 3.20)
bullets: Light going from denser to less dense medium
Angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
teach.note: Then no refracted ray at all.

teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Glass has refractive index 1.5. Find its critical angle.

teach.heading: Uses

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Water has n = 1.33. Its critical angle is about...

practice.a: From denser to less dense medium; angle of incidence greater than the critical angle

practice.q: Why do glass prisms in binoculars work at 45°?
practice.a: 45° is greater than glass's critical angle (about 42°), so TIR occurs

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 7 marks): An optical fibre has core n = 1.48. (a) Calculate the critical angle [3]. (b) Explain how light travels along a curved fibre [3]. (c) Give one use [1].
independent.a: (a) sin c = 1/1.48 (1) = 0.676 (1); c = 42.5° (1); (b) light hits the core boundary at more than c (1), totally internally reflected (1), repeatedly along the fibre (1); (c) communications or endoscopes (1)
independent.model: Teacher sets out (a): sin c = 1 ÷ 1.48.

independent.q: Extend: A ray in glass (n = 1.5) hits the surface at 35°. What happens and why? [2 marks]
independent.a: It refracts out (with some reflection) (1) because 35° is less than the critical angle of 42° (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Find n for a material whose critical angle is 30°.

exit.q: TIR needs i ... c.
Big question: why doesn't light leak out of an optical fibre?
exit.a: It always meets the boundary above the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected.

hook.text: An ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it drives away, but the driver hears no change. Why?
hook.a: Waves bunch up in front of a moving source (shorter wavelength, higher frequency) and spread out behind it; the driver moves with the source.

starter.q: v = fλ: 340 m/s, 170 Hz gives λ = ?

teach.heading: Sound (spec 3.23)
bullets: Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to energy transfer
teach.note: Slinky push-pull demonstration.

teach.heading: Reflection and refraction of sound
teach.note: Air about 340 m/s; water about 1500 m/s.

teach.heading: The Doppler effect (spec 3.8)
bullets: Moving away: longer λ, lower f
teach.note: Applies to all waves, including light (red-shift is Physics-only).

teach.heading: Echo calculation
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: A clap echoes from a cliff 170 m away. Sound travels at 340 m/s. Find the echo time.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: A car approaches you sounding its horn at 400 Hz. You hear...
check.why: Waves are compressed in front of the moving source, so the observed frequency is higher.

practice.q: Explain why sound cannot travel in a vacuum. [2 marks]
practice.a: Sound is a vibration of particles (1); a vacuum has no particles to pass on the vibrations (1)
practice.model: What carries sound? Vibrating particles of a medium. What is in a vacuum? Nothing. So no vibrations can pass on.

practice.q: Echo returns after 0.4 s at 340 m/s. Distance to the wall?
What happens to the observed wavelength as a source moves away?

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): A train sounds a horn of frequency 500 Hz. (a) Describe and explain what a person on the platform hears as the train approaches and then passes [4]. (b) Calculate the wavelength of the 500 Hz sound in still air at 340 m/s [2].
independent.a: (a) higher pitch as it approaches (1) because wavefronts are compressed/shorter wavelength (1); lower pitch after passing (1) because wavelength is stretched (1); (b) λ = 340 ÷ 500 = 0.68 m (2)
independent.model: Teacher answers the first mark: 'As the train approaches, the person hears a higher frequency than 500 Hz.'

independent.q: Extend: Why does sound travel faster in water than in air? [2 marks]
independent.a: Particles are closer together (1), so vibrations are passed on more quickly (1)

independent.q: Stretch: How do police speed guns use the Doppler effect?
independent.a: They measure the frequency change of reflected radio or microwave signals from a moving car to calculate its speed.

exit.q: Sound waves are made of compressions and...
Big question: why does the siren pitch change for you but not the driver?
exit.a: The source moves towards or away from you, changing the wavelength you receive; the driver moves with it.

independent.q: Extend: Compare the speed of response to touching a hot object and to a rise in blood glucose. [2 marks]

lessons.title: Homeostasis: temperature control
lessons.bigQuestion: You can stand in a sauna at 80 °C or in snow at -5 °C, yet your core stays near 37 °C. How?
objectives: To understand how the skin keeps body temperature constant through homeostasis
successCriteria: All: define homeostasis and give two examples
Most: describe sweating, vasodilation and vasoconstriction
Some: explain how the body responds when too hot or too cold
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: energy transfer by evaporation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: balance placed in the body

keywords.def: keeping internal conditions constant
widening of blood vessels near the skin surface
narrowing of blood vessels near the skin surface
releasing sweat whose evaporation cools the skin
control of body temperature

hook.text: You can stand in a sauna at 80 °C or in snow at -5 °C, yet your core stays near 37 °C. How?
hook.a: Homeostasis: the brain detects changes and the skin responds by sweating, shivering and changing blood flow.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'He who created you, proportioned you and balanced you' (Al-Infitar 82:7). The body's constant balancing of its temperature is part of that creation in balance.

teach.heading: Homeostasis (spec 2.81)
bullets: Water content and temperature are examples
teach.note: Changes are detected and corrected.

teach.heading: Too hot (spec 2.93)
bullets: Vasodilation: more blood near surface, more heat lost
teach.note: Skin looks flushed.

teach.heading: Too cold (spec 2.93)
teach.note: Skin looks pale.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Examiners penalise 'vessels move'.

misconception.wrong: Blood vessels move closer to the skin surface when we are hot.
misconception.right: Arterioles near the surface dilate, letting more blood flow near the surface; vessels do not move.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Shivering helps warm the body because...
options: Muscles contract, respiring and releasing heat
check.why: Muscle contraction needs respiration, which releases energy as heat.

practice.q: Explain how sweating cools the body. [2 marks]
practice.a: Sweat evaporates from the skin (1), transferring energy from the skin to the surroundings (1)
practice.model: Sweat is water on the skin. It evaporates. Evaporation needs energy, taken from the skin. So the skin cools.

practice.q: What is vasoconstriction?
practice.a: Narrowing of blood vessels near the skin surface

practice.q: Name two conditions kept constant by homeostasis.
practice.a: Body temperature and water content (also blood glucose)

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe and explain how the body responds when a person walks into a very cold place. Portal response box.
independent.a: Temperature receptors detect the fall (1); brain coordinates (1); vasoconstriction (1) reduces blood flow near the surface, less heat lost (1); shivering (1) muscles respire releasing heat (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes: 'Temperature receptors detect that the body is cooling.'

independent.q: Extend: Why is sweating less effective in humid air? [2 marks]
independent.a: Air is already full of water vapour (1), so sweat evaporates slowly and less heat is lost (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why can a high fever be dangerous?
independent.a: Enzymes may denature above about 40 °C, so metabolism is disrupted.

exit.q: When hot, blood vessels near the skin...
Big question: how does your core stay near 37 °C?
exit.a: Homeostasis: sweating, shivering, vasodilation and vasoconstriction controlled by the brain.

hook.text: Bee stings are acidic and wasp stings alkaline, so folk remedies use bicarbonate for one and vinegar for the other. What idea are they using?

independent.a: (a) vinegar, lemon acidic; water neutral; bicarbonate alkaline (2); (b) H⁺ from acid react with OH⁻ (or the base) (1) to form water; pH rises to 7 (1); (c) phenolphthalein (1); (d) about 3 (1)

independent.q: Extend: Explain why indigestion tablets contain bases. [2 marks]

independent.a: Each pH unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration, so pH 1 has ten times the H⁺ of pH 2 (the scale is logarithmic).

exit.q: Alkalis produce ... ions in water.

exit.a: Neutralisation: an alkali cancels an acid, an acid cancels an alkali.
